topics.name: Absent-Mindedness / Everyday Attention-Memory Lapses
topics.description: Lapses in attention and memory during routine, well-practiced tasks, distinct from a specific named cognitive bias.

biases.name: Absent-Mindedness
biases.description: Absent-mindedness is a family of everyday memory failures caused by lapses of attention: the mind is elsewhere when information or an intended action should be encoded or retrieved. It often shows up as misplacing things, forgetting routine intentions, or losing track of what one was doing mid-task.

topics.name: Attentional Bias
topics.description: A tendency for attention to be disproportionately drawn to certain stimuli (e.g. threat-related cues), shaping what information a person notices and processes before any deliberate judgment occurs.

biases.name: Attentional Bias
biases.description: A person's attention is pulled disproportionately toward certain kinds of stimuli rather than distributed evenly across what is present. In practice this usually means emotionally charged, threatening, craving-related, or goal-relevant cues get noticed first and held longer.

topics.name: Banner Blindness
topics.description: Whether users actually see distinctive, highlighted web elements — they largely don't, but the ads/banners they don't consciously register still measurably cost attention and working memory, directly relevant to how much a design should rely on visual salience alone to communicate.

biases.name: Selective Attention
biases.description: People attend to only a small subset of the stimuli available to them, usually the ones most relevant to their current goal. Fully visible interface elements can still go unnoticed when attention is already committed elsewhere.

standalone_findings.description: Eye-tracking confirmed people rarely look directly at banner ads at all — but the presence of banners, especially animated ones, still measurably increased perceived cognitive workload and slowed visual search for other content, even when the banner itself went unseen. Animated banners were also, surprisingly, harder to remember afterward than static look-alikes. Banner blindness doesn't mean banners are cost-free — just that the cost isn't paid through the attention they were designed to capture.
standalone_findings.source_title: High-Cost Banner Blindness

topics.name: Change Blindness
topics.description: The failure to notice large changes in a scene when the change coincides with a visual disruption (a blink, a cut, a blank frame) — directly relevant to why users miss UI changes that happen during a transition or reload.

biases.name: Change Blindness
biases.description: People are strikingly poor at detecting even large changes to a scene when the moment of change itself is masked (e.g. by a blink, cut, or blank flash), because attention, not raw visual exposure, is what makes a change perceptible from one glance to the next.

topics.name: Choice Blindness
topics.description: Whether people notice when the outcome of their own stated choice or preference is covertly swapped — they mostly don't, and will often confabulate reasons for a choice they never actually made. Directly relevant to how much weight self-reported preference data in user research and survey validation actually deserves.

biases.name: Choice Blindness
biases.description: People frequently fail to notice when the outcome of their own choice is covertly swapped for the option they rejected, and will go on to confidently construct coherent reasons defending a preference they never actually held -- a direct challenge to the reliability of introspective self-report about one's own preferences and reasons.

topics.name: Functional Fixedness
topics.description: Fixating on an object's conventional, familiar use, which blocks recognizing alternative or creative uses for it in problem-solving.

biases.name: Functional Fixedness
biases.description: Once an object or interface element is strongly associated with its usual function, people can struggle to see other possible uses. Familiar purpose becomes a cognitive constraint on creative problem solving.

standalone_findings.description: Functional fixedness was demonstrated in Shuar adolescents of Ecuadorian Amazonia -- a technologically sparse culture with limited access to artifacts with many specialized functions -- using the same style of object-repurposing problem-solving task as the classic Western studies. Suggests that fixation on an object's design function is not an artifact of Western technological abundance, but may be a universal property of how artifact concepts are represented in human semantic memory.
standalone_findings.source_title: Functional Fixedness in a Technologically Sparse Culture

standalone_findings.description: Older children (6- and 7-year-olds) showed functional fixedness (slower to repurpose a box as a support after its containment function was demonstrated), but 5-year-olds were immune -- showing no disadvantage from prior functional demonstration, and outperforming the older groups even under that condition. Suggests functional fixedness is acquired through increasing experience with objects' conventional uses rather than being an innate cognitive constraint.
standalone_findings.source_title: Immunity to functional fixedness in young children

topics.name: Inattentional Blindness
topics.description: The failure to see something fully visible because attention was focused elsewhere — the 'gorilla' experiment, with a real applied extension showing public-display interfaces are noticed by intent-driven users far more than incidentally-present ones.

biases.name: Selective Attention
biases.description: People attend to only a small subset of the stimuli available to them, usually the ones most relevant to their current goal. Fully visible interface elements can still go unnoticed when attention is already committed elsewhere.

standalone_findings.description: In a field study of public information interfaces, users who arrived with an intent to actively seek information ('direct users') reported noticing up to 68% of the interfaces shown to them, while users who were otherwise engaged and merely passing through ('indirect users') noticed only 16% — demonstrating that inattentional blindness can be deliberately exploited (or must be actively designed against) to make an interface, notification, or UI element noticeable only to users who are already looking for it.
standalone_findings.source_title: To See or Not to See: Exploring Inattentional Blindness for the Design of Public Interfaces
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (IMWUT)

topics.name: Pareidolia
topics.description: Perceiving a specific, often meaningful pattern — commonly faces — in random or ambiguous visual or auditory stimuli.

biases.name: Pareidolia
biases.description: People can perceive specific meaningful patterns—most famously faces—in random, noisy, or ambiguous stimuli. The mind completes a recognisable signal that is not objectively there.

standalone_findings.description: Proverbio & Galli independently confirm face pareidolia's neural signature using ERPs: the face-specific N170 component over the right hemisphere was larger in response to faces-in-things (FITs) than to matched objects, replicating the selective neural recruitment for illusory faces that Liu et al. found via fMRI/fusiform-face-area activation, though using real ambiguous objects rather than pure-noise-generated stimuli. A secondary finding not in the original study: a sex difference in a later ERP component (VPP) during FIT processing.
standalone_findings.source_title: Women are better at seeing faces where there are none: an ERP study of face pareidolia

topics.name: Processing Disfluency / Disfluency Effect
topics.description: Information that is harder to process or read is sometimes (though not consistently) judged as more important, memorable, or effortful/valuable than more fluently-processed information.

biases.name: Processing Difficulty Effect
biases.description: Information that is harder to process can sometimes feel more effortful, serious, or valuable than easy-to-process information. But the effect is not one clean rule: difficulty can also backfire, confuse, or reduce trust depending on the task.

standalone_findings.description: A direct methodological re-examination of Xie, Zhou & Liu's (2018) disfluency meta-analysis found its transfer-performance conclusions held up as reasonably robust under reproducibility checks, but identified real coding/effect-size errors and reproducibility problems specifically affecting the recall-performance results and moderator analysis -- an honest, partial complication rather than a wholesale rejection of the null-effects finding.
standalone_findings.source_title: Null and Void? Errors in Meta-analysis on Perceptual Disfluency and Recommendations to Improve Meta-analytical Reproducibility

topics.name: Rhyme-as-Reason Effect / Keats Heuristic
topics.description: Statements phrased in rhyme are judged as more accurate or truthful than logically equivalent statements in non-rhyming form.

biases.name: Rhyme-as-Reason Effect
biases.description: Statements phrased in rhyme can feel truer or more valid than semantically equivalent non-rhyming versions. The verbal form itself gets mistaken for evidence.

topics.name: Self-Report & Preference-Data Reliability in User Research
topics.description: The design-practice angle on choice blindness: if people confabulate reasons for choices they never made, how much should a user-research debrief, an A/B test rationale, or a survey response actually be trusted as a window into why someone really chose something.

biases.name: Choice Blindness
biases.description: People frequently fail to notice when the outcome of their own choice is covertly swapped for the option they rejected, and will go on to confidently construct coherent reasons defending a preference they never actually held -- a direct challenge to the reliability of introspective self-report about one's own preferences and reasons.

domains.name: Choice Architecture
domains.description: How structuring the option set itself — defaults, category counts — shapes what gets chosen.

topics.name: Boosts vs. Nudges
topics.description: Hertwig & Grüne-Yanoff's distinction between nudges (which exploit cognitive biases to steer behavior) and boosts (which instead aim to improve people's own decision-making competence) — a direct theoretical alternative to the general nudging literature.

standalone_findings.description: Boosts and nudges are conceptually distinct classes of behavioral policy intervention, not two labels for the same thing: they differ in immediate intervention target (boosts target competence/decision-making tools; nudges target behavior directly), theoretical roots (boosts draw on the 'simple heuristics' / ecological-rationality research program; nudges draw on the heuristics-and-biases program), causal pathway (boosts work through changing a person's repertoire of skills/knowledge/decision tools; nudges work by exploiting existing cognitive biases or default psychological responses), assumed cognitive architecture, reversibility of effects once the intervention is withdrawn (boost effects are argued to persist; nudge effects are argued to typically require the nudge to remain in place), programmatic ambition, and normative/autonomy implications.
standalone_findings.source_title: Nudging and Boosting: Steering or Empowering Good Decisions

topics.name: Choice Architecture & Nudging (General)
topics.description: The broad choice-architecture/nudging literature covering overall effectiveness claims, cutting across specific techniques and domains.

biases.name: Nudge
biases.description: Choice architecture -- how options are structured, defaulted, or framed -- can shift behavior without restricting choice or changing economic incentives. Overall effect sizes reported in the literature range from small-to-medium to functionally near-zero depending on how publication bias is corrected for, and effectiveness varies widely by intervention type and context.

standalone_findings.description: Boosts and nudges are conceptually distinct classes of behavioral policy intervention, not two labels for the same thing: they differ in immediate intervention target (boosts target competence/decision-making tools; nudges target behavior directly), theoretical roots (boosts draw on the 'simple heuristics' / ecological-rationality research program; nudges draw on the heuristics-and-biases program), causal pathway (boosts work through changing a person's repertoire of skills/knowledge/decision tools; nudges work by exploiting existing cognitive biases or default psychological responses), assumed cognitive architecture, reversibility of effects once the intervention is withdrawn (boost effects are argued to persist; nudge effects are argued to typically require the nudge to remain in place), programmatic ambition, and normative/autonomy implications.
standalone_findings.source_title: Nudging and Boosting: Steering or Empowering Good Decisions

topics.name: Choice Overload / Paradox of Choice
topics.description: Whether more available options reduce decision motivation and satisfaction ('choice overload' / 'paradox of choice') — a claim treated as settled in design/business practice but genuinely disputed in the underlying meta-analytic literature.

biases.name: Choice Overload
biases.description: Beyond a certain point, more options reduce rather than increase the likelihood of choosing at all, and reduce satisfaction with whatever is chosen.

topics.name: Default Effects
topics.description: Pre-selected/default options in a choice architecture, and their outsized effect on which option people end up choosing.

biases.name: Default Effect
biases.description: The pre-selected option in a choice is disproportionately likely to be chosen, independent of its objective merits.

biases.name: Status Quo Bias
biases.description: People disproportionately prefer to keep things the way they are, even when a switch would be objectively beneficial and low-cost.

standalone_findings.description: A pre-commitment savings program (Save More Tomorrow), where employees commit in advance to allocating future salary increases toward retirement savings, substantially increased savings rates across its first three real-world implementations.
standalone_findings.effect_size: Substantially increased savings rates (see paper for firm-level figures)
standalone_findings.source_title: Save More Tomorrow™: Using Behavioral Economics to Increase Employee Saving

topics.name: Less-Is-Better Effect
topics.description: An option is judged more favorably when evaluated alone than when evaluated jointly alongside a superior alternative, reversing the usual preference once direct comparison is possible.

biases.name: Less-Is-Better Effect
biases.description: An option can look better when judged on its own than it does when compared side by side with an objectively superior alternative. Separate evaluation can reverse what feels better because people lean on different cues when direct comparison is absent.

topics.name: Libertarian Paternalism (Philosophy & Policy)
topics.description: The philosophical/policy position that choice architecture inevitably shapes decisions, and that this can be done while preserving freedom of choice — the normative framework underlying most nudge policy arguments.

biases.name: Libertarian Paternalism
biases.description: The position that choice architects can and should steer people's decisions toward outcomes that improve their own welfare, while preserving each person's freedom to choose otherwise -- the foundational philosophical framework behind 'nudge' interventions.

topics.name: Savings & Retirement Behavior
topics.description: Behavioral interventions targeting retirement/long-term savings decisions specifically, including commitment devices.

standalone_findings.description: A pre-commitment savings program (Save More Tomorrow), where employees commit in advance to allocating future salary increases toward retirement savings, substantially increased savings rates across its first three real-world implementations.
standalone_findings.effect_size: Substantially increased savings rates (see paper for firm-level figures)
standalone_findings.source_title: Save More Tomorrow™: Using Behavioral Economics to Increase Employee Saving

standalone_findings.description: Human time preferences are better described by a hyperbolic (quasi-hyperbolic, present-biased) discount function than by the classical exponential-discounting model of economics — implying people place disproportionately high weight on immediate rewards relative to future ones, explaining undersaving and self-control problems and motivating commitment-device interventions.
standalone_findings.source_title: Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting

topics.name: Sludge (Friction as Anti-Nudge)
topics.description: Friction deliberately or incidentally added to a process that makes a beneficial action harder — the structural inverse of a nudge, and Sunstein's proposed 'sludge audit' as an institutional accounting practice for finding it.

biases.name: Sludge
biases.description: Friction, excessive paperwork, or other choice-architecture features that make it needlessly difficult for people to take an action that serves their own interest -- unenrolling from a subscription, claiming a benefit, canceling a service -- the deliberate or negligent opposite of a helpful nudge.

topics.name: Status Quo Bias
topics.description: The tendency to prefer the current state of affairs over switching, even when switching is low-cost and objectively beneficial.

biases.name: Status Quo Bias
biases.description: People disproportionately prefer to keep things the way they are, even when a switch would be objectively beneficial and low-cost.

biases.name: System Justification
biases.description: People are motivated to see existing institutions, hierarchies, and arrangements as legitimate and fair, even when those arrangements disadvantage them. That motive can make the status quo feel natural, deserved, or harder to challenge than it objectively is.

domains.name: Design Ethics & Misuse
domains.description: The normative layer: when persuasive/behavioral techniques cross into manipulation.

topics.name: Dark Patterns & Design Ethics
topics.description: Manipulative interface design patterns that exploit cognitive biases to produce outcomes users wouldn't otherwise choose — the real-world misuse side of persuasive design.

biases.name: Reactance
biases.description: When people feel their freedom or autonomy is being threatened, they resist, push back, or sometimes do the opposite of what is being urged. Pressure can reduce compliance precisely because it feels controlling.

standalone_findings.description: A cross-country analysis of popular news sites found a modern 'Roach Motel' pattern in subscription design: signing up online is straightforward, but cancellation flows often add intentional barriers such as forcing users to call a representative or type a required phrase, while many subscription flows also fail to adequately disclose recurring charges. The paper frames these obstacles as manipulative dark patterns that persist even in the context of recent regulation.
standalone_findings.source_title: Staying at the Roach Motel: Cross-Country Analysis of Manipulative Subscription and Cancellation Flows
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems

standalone_findings.description: An automated crawl of ~53K product pages across ~11K shopping websites found 1,818 dark pattern instances across 15 types and 7 broader categories; 183 websites engaged in outright deceptive practices; 22 third-party vendors offer dark patterns as a turnkey commercial solution.
standalone_findings.source_title: Dark Patterns at Scale: Findings from a Crawl of 11K Shopping Websites
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (CSCW)

standalone_findings.description: In two large-scale experiments with representative U.S. consumer samples, users exposed to mild dark patterns were more than twice as likely to sign up for a dubious service as a control group; users exposed to aggressive dark patterns were almost four times as likely — and aggressive patterns triggered strong consumer backlash while mild ones did not.
standalone_findings.effect_size: ~2x (mild dark patterns) / ~4x (aggressive dark patterns) increase in dubious-service signup rate vs. control
standalone_findings.source_title: Shining a Light on Dark Patterns

standalone_findings.description: Post-GDPR cookie-consent interfaces still use dark patterns at scale: scraping the five most popular CMP designs across the top 10,000 UK websites found only 11.8% of observed consent pop-ups met the authors' minimal legal requirements, and a field experiment showed that removing the opt-out button from the first page increased consent by 22-23 percentage points while exposing more granular controls on the first page reduced consent by 8-20 percentage points. Whether the notice appeared as a banner or a barrier did not materially change consent.
standalone_findings.effect_size: Only 11.8% of sampled CMP pop-ups met minimal legal requirements; removing the opt-out button increased consent by 22-23 percentage points; more granular first-page controls reduced consent by 8-20 percentage points
standalone_findings.source_title: Dark Patterns after the GDPR: Scraping Consent Pop-ups and Demonstrating their Influence
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the 2020 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems

standalone_findings.description: Proposes explicit ethical guidelines for digital nudge design (transparency of intent, preserving genuine freedom of choice, avoiding exploitation of cognitive vulnerabilities) as a direct response to the growing overlap and confusion between legitimate 'digital nudging' and manipulative dark-pattern design in practice.
standalone_findings.source_title: Ethical Guidelines for the Construction of Digital Nudges
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the 53rd Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS)

standalone_findings.description: The EDPB's final Guidelines 03/2022 define deceptive design patterns in social-media platform interfaces as interface/user-journey choices that steer users toward unintended, privacy-harmful decisions and classify them into six high-level families: Overloading, Skipping, Stirring, Obstructing, Fickle, and Left in the Dark. Each family is broken into named subtypes (for example, Continuous Prompting, Privacy Maze, Emotional Steering, Misleading Action, Language Discontinuity, and Ambiguous Wording/Information), showing how the dark-pattern taxonomy expanded after 2019 into a GDPR-specific regulatory vocabulary.
standalone_findings.source_title: Guidelines 03/2022 on deceptive design patterns in social media platform interfaces: how to recognise and avoid them

standalone_findings.description: The FTC's 2022 staff report argues that dark patterns have migrated online at much greater scale and sophistication than their offline predecessors and organizes the main consumer-protection problems into concrete buckets: inducing false beliefs, hiding or obscuring material information, tricking people into unauthorized or recurring charges, and creating roadblocks to cancellation. The report also stresses that dark patterns are often combined, which compounds harm beyond the effect of any single tactic in isolation.
standalone_findings.source_title: Bringing Dark Patterns to Light
standalone_findings.source_venue: Federal Trade Commission (Bureau of Consumer Protection staff report)

topics.name: Design with Intent (Behavior-Change Design Methods)
topics.description: A design-ideation method for translating a behavior-change goal into concrete product/system design concepts.

biases.name: Design with Intent
biases.description: A design method and toolkit for deliberately influencing user behavior through interface and product design choices, organized into distinct 'lenses' (e.g. architectural, security, persuasive, visual, cognitive) that a designer can apply to intentionally shape how people interact with a system.

topics.name: Digital Nudging & HCI Design Ethics
topics.description: How nudging concepts get applied specifically in software/interface design, and the ethical guidelines proposed to keep that application legitimate rather than manipulative.

biases.name: Digital Nudging
biases.description: The deliberate use of interface and interaction design elements (defaults, framing, presentation order, incentives) within digital environments to steer users toward a particular choice -- the online-product-specific application of nudge theory, distinguished from offline nudging by its capacity for personalization, scale, and A/B-tested optimization against a target metric.

standalone_findings.description: A systematic review of nudging techniques used in HCI/technology-mediated design research identifies 6 core cognitive-bias mechanisms and 23 distinct nudge design techniques, but finds the field lacks consensus on how to reliably design for and evaluate nudge effectiveness — many published applications don't clearly report which underlying mechanism they actually target.
standalone_findings.source_title: 23 Ways to Nudge
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the 2019 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (ACM)

topics.name: Libertarian Paternalism (Philosophy & Policy)
topics.description: The philosophical/policy position that choice architecture inevitably shapes decisions, and that this can be done while preserving freedom of choice — the normative framework underlying most nudge policy arguments.

biases.name: Libertarian Paternalism
biases.description: The position that choice architects can and should steer people's decisions toward outcomes that improve their own welfare, while preserving each person's freedom to choose otherwise -- the foundational philosophical framework behind 'nudge' interventions.

topics.name: Psychological Reactance
topics.description: People resist or reverse a persuasion attempt when they perceive their freedom of choice as being threatened — directly relevant to why heavy-handed persuasive/dark-pattern tactics can backfire.

biases.name: Reactance
biases.description: When people feel their freedom or autonomy is being threatened, they resist, push back, or sometimes do the opposite of what is being urged. Pressure can reduce compliance precisely because it feels controlling.

biases.name: Reverse Psychology
biases.description: A persuader deliberately recommends or allows the opposite of the desired outcome in hopes that the target will push back and choose the originally desired behavior instead. It is a tactic, not a basic cognitive mechanism by itself.

topics.name: Sludge (Friction as Anti-Nudge)
topics.description: Friction deliberately or incidentally added to a process that makes a beneficial action harder — the structural inverse of a nudge, and Sunstein's proposed 'sludge audit' as an institutional accounting practice for finding it.

biases.name: Sludge
biases.description: Friction, excessive paperwork, or other choice-architecture features that make it needlessly difficult for people to take an action that serves their own interest -- unenrolling from a subscription, claiming a benefit, canceling a service -- the deliberate or negligent opposite of a helpful nudge.

domains.name: Evidentiary Rigor & Meta-Science
domains.description: The trustworthiness of the science itself, independent of subject matter.

topics.name: Backfire Effect
topics.description: The contested claim that correcting a false belief can sometimes strengthen it rather than weaken it — recent large-scale replications have mostly failed to reproduce this beyond narrow conditions.

biases.name: Backfire Effect
biases.description: Corrections aimed at debunking a false belief can, in some cases, strengthen commitment to the original belief instead of weakening it. In the current literature, the stronger claim that factual corrections usually backfire appears much shakier and more contingent than the label suggests.

standalone_findings.description: The peer-reviewed misinformation literature reviewed here shows that retracted misinformation often continues to shape memory and reasoning even after the correction is understood and remembered; providing alternative causal explanations helps, but persistence remains a recurring problem.
standalone_findings.source_title: Misinformation and Its Correction
standalone_findings.source_venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest

topics.name: Cognitive Bias Taxonomies for Design Practice
topics.description: Academic attempts to organize the large, diffuse space of cognitive biases into taxonomies usable by a specific design discipline (e.g. data visualization), rather than by abstract cognitive theory — the direct precedent for this project's own BiasHeuristic taxonomy.

standalone_findings.description: Proposes a task-based taxonomy of 154 cognitive biases relevant to information visualization design, organized into 7 categories by which analysis/visualization task they affect — explicitly built to be more usable for designers than prior bias taxonomies organized around abstract cognitive theory, while noting limited empirical research documents how most of these biases actually affect real visual data analysis activities.
standalone_findings.source_title: A Task-Based Taxonomy of Cognitive Biases for Information Visualization
standalone_findings.source_venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

topics.name: Continued Influence Effect
topics.description: Misinformation continues to shape a person's reasoning even after they've received and acknowledged a credible correction.

biases.name: Continued Influence Effect
biases.description: Misinformation can keep shaping memory and reasoning even after a correction is seen, understood, and remembered. A bare retraction often does not fully remove the old story's causal grip.

topics.name: Cross-Cultural Replication of Framing & Anchoring Effects
topics.description: Whether classic framing and anchoring effects, originally demonstrated in single Western samples, actually replicate outside them — Many Labs 2's 36-country direct replication of the gain/loss framing paradigm found the effect held in the same direction, though at reduced magnitude.

biases.name: Cross-Cultural Robustness of Framing & Anchoring Effects
biases.description: At least some classic judgment effects designers borrow from behavioral economics do not appear to be limited to Western student samples. The safest reading here is meta-scientific: framing clearly held directionally across many countries, while the anchoring side is genuinely more mixed -- present, but not a clean universal replication.

topics.name: Cross-Cultural Variation in Loss Aversion
topics.description: Whether loss aversion's magnitude is a universal human parameter or varies systematically with culture — a 53-country survey found it varies predictably with individualism, power distance, masculinity, and religious composition.

biases.name: Loss Aversion
biases.description: Losses loom psychologically larger than equivalent gains — people work harder to avoid losing something than to gain the equivalent.

topics.name: Experimenter Bias / Observer-Expectancy Effect
topics.description: A researcher's own expectations can unintentionally influence how they interact with participants or interpret data, biasing results toward the expected outcome.

biases.name: Experimenter Bias
biases.description: A researcher's expectations can unintentionally shape what participants do or how outcomes are observed, recorded, or interpreted. The study starts leaning toward the hoped-for answer before the analysis even begins.

topics.name: Hawthorne Effect / Research Participation Effects
topics.description: Being aware of being observed or studied can itself change a participant's behavior, independent of any actual experimental manipulation.

biases.name: Observer Effect
biases.description: In the social-science sense, people may change their behavior because they know they are being observed or studied. This entry is about behavioral reactivity, not the physics meaning of measurement disturbing a system.

topics.name: Memory Suggestibility / Misinformation Effect
topics.description: Memory can be altered by suggestion, leading questions, or misleading post-event information, so a later recollection incorporates the suggested content as if it were originally experienced.

biases.name: Suggestibility
biases.description: Memory can be altered by suggestion, leading questions, or misleading post-event information. The person's later recollection may incorporate the suggestion as if it were part of the original experience.

standalone_findings.description: The same review concludes that people can come to believe falsely that they experienced rich, complex events that never in fact occurred, showing that false memory can extend beyond minor detail distortion to invented episodes under some conditions.
standalone_findings.source_title: Planting misinformation in the human mind: a 30-year investigation of the malleability of memory.

topics.name: Power Posing
topics.description: The (contested) claim that adopting expansive body postures causes measurable hormonal and behavioral changes.

biases.name: Power Posing
biases.description: The popular claim that briefly holding an expansive, 'high-power' body posture changes a person's hormone levels (raising testosterone, lowering cortisol) and increases their real-world risk tolerance and confidence -- one of psychology's most publicly famous claims (via a widely-viewed TED talk), and one of its most publicly disputed.

standalone_findings.description: Adopting expansive ('high-power') body postures for brief periods caused measurable increases in testosterone, decreases in cortisol, and increased self-reported feelings of power and risk tolerance, compared to contractive ('low-power') postures.
standalone_findings.source_title: Power Posing: Brief Nonverbal Displays Affect Neuroendocrine Levels and Risk Tolerance

topics.name: Publication Bias & Methodological Rigor
topics.description: How much the published behavioral-science literature overstates true effect sizes due to selective publication of positive results, and the methodological practices (power analysis, preregistration) that would detect or prevent it.

biases.name: Publication Bias
biases.description: The tendency for studies with positive, statistically significant, or novel results to be published, cited, and built upon far more readily than studies with null or inconclusive results -- systematically inflating the apparent size and reliability of an effect in the published literature relative to its true magnitude.

standalone_findings.description: A large-scale coordinated replication of 100 psychology experiments from top journals found only about 36% of replications produced statistically significant results matching the original (vs. 97% of the original studies), with replication effect sizes averaging roughly half the magnitude of the original studies.
standalone_findings.effect_size: 36% of replications significant (vs. 97% originals); ~50% average effect-size retention
standalone_findings.source_title: Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science

standalone_findings.description: A systematic integrative review spanning four decades of decoy-effect research finds no clear scientific consensus on the underlying mechanism and documents substantial heterogeneity in when and how strongly the effect manifests across contexts — a caution against treating the decoy effect as a uniformly reliable design lever.
standalone_findings.source_title: An integrative review of the decoy effect on choice behavior

standalone_findings.description: An independent large-scale replication project (21 experimental social-science studies from Nature and Science, 2010–2015) found only 62% replicated with a statistically significant effect in the same direction, and replication effect sizes averaged about 50% of the original — corroborating a broad, cross-disciplinary replication-rate problem rather than one specific to a single journal or subfield.
standalone_findings.effect_size: 62% replicated significant, same direction; ~50% average effect-size retention
standalone_findings.source_title: Evaluating the replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science between 2010 and 2015

standalone_findings.description: When experimental procedures are modified to remove subject misconceptions about the valuation-elicitation mechanism (anonymity, incentive-compatible training), the willingness-to-pay/willingness-to-accept gap largely disappears — suggesting much of the originally observed 'endowment effect' may reflect procedural artifacts and subject confusion rather than a stable psychological effect.
standalone_findings.source_title: The Willingness to Pay–Willingness to Accept Gap, the "Endowment Effect," Subject Misconceptions, and Experimental Procedures for Eliciting Valuations

biases.name: Choice Blindness
biases.description: People frequently fail to notice when the outcome of their own choice is covertly swapped for the option they rejected, and will go on to confidently construct coherent reasons defending a preference they never actually held -- a direct challenge to the reliability of introspective self-report about one's own preferences and reasons.

topics.name: Social Desirability Bias
topics.description: Over-reporting socially approved attitudes/behaviors and under-reporting disapproved ones in self-report data — directly relevant to the reliability of self-reported UX research findings.

biases.name: Social Desirability Bias
biases.description: When asked to describe themselves, people often overreport socially approved behaviors and underreport disapproved ones. The answer shifts toward what sounds good, not just what is true.

standalone_findings.description: A literature review of social desirability bias in sensitive surveys finds the phenomenon is driven by a combination of psychological factors (a stable need for social approval, avoidance of embarrassing social interactions), survey-design characteristics, interviewer characteristics, and the survey situation itself. Reviews the empirical evidence on which specific survey methods actually reduce socially desirable misreporting, concluding that survey designers can improve data validity by selecting data-collection strategies that reduce respondent discomfort with sensitive questions.
standalone_findings.source_title: Determinants of social desirability bias in sensitive surveys: a literature review

standalone_findings.description: A meta-analysis of 460 effect sizes (N=125,672) found computerized self-administered surveys elicited significantly more honest reporting of socially undesirable behaviors than equivalent paper-and-pencil surveys -- the effect was strongest for highly sensitive behaviors and individually-administered surveys. No interviewer effects were found, and audio-enhanced computer surveys offered no additional benefit. Directly informs UX/survey research methodology: digital, self-administered survey modes measurably reduce social-desirability distortion relative to paper for sensitive topics.
standalone_findings.source_title: Disclosure of sensitive behaviors across self-administered survey modes: a meta-analysis

topics.name: Social Priming & the Replication Crisis
topics.description: Claims that subtle environmental or linguistic cues unconsciously shift subsequent behavior — one of the areas hit hardest by the replication crisis.

standalone_findings.description: Daniel Kahneman publicly acknowledged serious doubts about the replicability of social priming research — including specific studies (e.g. the 'Florida effect' walking-speed study) that he had cited approvingly in Thinking, Fast and Slow — and urged the field to address the problem directly.
standalone_findings.source_title: Nobel laureate challenges psychologists to clean up their act

topics.name: The Replication Crisis (Meta-Science)
topics.description: Field-wide, cross-disciplinary evidence on how often published psychology/behavioral-science findings actually replicate — the meta-scientific context behind many specific disputes elsewhere in this graph.

biases.name: The Replication Crisis
biases.description: Large-scale, coordinated attempts to directly replicate published psychology findings have repeatedly found that only roughly a third to two-thirds of original results reproduce with a statistically significant effect in the same direction, and that replicated effect sizes typically shrink to about half the originally published magnitude -- a systemic, field-wide pattern documented across multiple independent large-scale projects, not an isolated embarrassment confined to a few disproven studies.

standalone_findings.description: A better-powered direct replication of the power-posing paradigm found postures did affect self-reported feelings of power, but found no evidence for effects on testosterone, cortisol, or behavioral risk tolerance — the original study's headline hormonal/behavioral claims specifically.
standalone_findings.source_title: Assessing the Robustness of Power Posing

standalone_findings.description: A large-scale preregistered replication (23 labs, N≈2,141) of the standard ego-depletion sequential-task paradigm found no significant depletion effect, directly contradicting the original resource-depletion model's central prediction.
standalone_findings.source_title: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect

topics.name: WEIRD Samples & Generalizability
topics.description: The critique that most behavioral-science findings come from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic samples that are a poor proxy for humans generally — a meta-science check on how far the rest of this corpus's findings actually generalize, not just another topic alongside them.

biases.name: WEIRD Samples Critique
biases.description: The overwhelming majority of published behavioral-science research draws its participant samples from Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic (WEIRD) societies -- a narrow and, on many measured psychological dimensions, statistically unusual slice of humanity -- meaning many 'universal' findings in the literature may not generalize as broadly as their framing implies.

topics.name: Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy
topics.description: The Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy (v1): a 93-technique, consensus-built classification for precisely specifying and reporting the active content of behavior-change interventions.

standalone_findings.description: A Delphi-type expert-consensus and reliability exercise produced 'BCT taxonomy v1': 93 distinct behaviour change techniques clustered into 16 groups. In the coding-reliability check, 23 of the 26 techniques that occurred at least five times achieved adjusted kappas of 0.60 or above, supporting the paper's claim that the taxonomy materially improves how intervention content can be specified and reported.
standalone_findings.effect_size: 93 BCTs in 16 groups; 23 of 26 frequently occurring techniques had adjusted kappa >= 0.60
standalone_findings.source_title: The Behavior Change Technique Taxonomy (v1) of 93 Hierarchically Clustered Techniques: Building an International Consensus for the Reporting of Behavior Change Interventions

topics.name: COM-B Model & Behavior Change Wheel
topics.description: Michie et al.'s COM-B model (capability, opportunity, motivation as the three conditions behavior requires) and the surrounding Behaviour Change Wheel framework for characterising and designing clinical/public-health behavior-change interventions.

standalone_findings.description: A systematic search plus expert consultation identified 19 existing behaviour-change-intervention frameworks spanning nine intervention functions and seven policy categories, but none covered the full range of intervention functions or policies, and only a minority were coherent or clearly linked to an overarching model of behaviour. Michie, van Stralen, and West present this as the concrete gap the Behaviour Change Wheel is meant to solve.
standalone_findings.effect_size: 19 frameworks identified; 9 intervention functions; 7 policy categories; none covered the full range
standalone_findings.source_title: The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions

standalone_findings.description: At the centre of the Behaviour Change Wheel is the COM-B system: behaviour is understood as requiring the interaction of three essential conditions — capability, opportunity, and motivation — and the framework's nine intervention functions are positioned explicitly as ways to address deficits in one or more of those conditions, with seven surrounding policy categories enabling those interventions.
standalone_findings.source_title: The behaviour change wheel: A new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions

topics.name: Construal Level Theory & Psychological Distance
topics.description: Trope & Liberman's theory that psychologically distant things — future, hypothetical, physically far, socially distant — are represented more abstractly than psychologically near things, and this shapes evaluation and decision-making.

standalone_findings.description: Psychological distance (temporal, spatial, social, and hypothetical) is a unified, egocentric construct: the farther an object or event is from the self in the here-and-now, the more abstractly (higher construal level) it is mentally represented, and the four distance dimensions are cognitively related to one another and similarly influence -- and are influenced by -- construal level, prediction, preference, and action.
standalone_findings.source_title: Construal-level theory of psychological distance

topics.name: Curiosity Gap (Information Gap Theory)
topics.description: Curiosity as a form of cognitively induced deprivation arising from a perceived gap between what someone knows and wants to know — the direct explanation for why deliberately withholding information drives engagement with headlines, previews, and progress indicators.

biases.name: Curiosity Gap
biases.description: A perceived gap between what someone knows and what they want to know creates an aversive state of deprivation that motivates information-seeking to close it.

standalone_findings.description: A corpus-linguistic analysis of clickbait headlines found writers create Loewenstein's 'information gap' via specific, statistically overrepresented parts-of-speech: definite referring expressions and superlatives/intensifiers. These constructions encourage readers to build new mental 'conceptual files' from the headline's terms while providing little actual content for them, driving readers to click in expectation of filling the gap. Directly explains the linguistic mechanics behind curiosity-gap-driven headline and notification copy in real design practice.
standalone_findings.source_title: You won't believe what's in this paper! Clickbait, relevance and the curiosity gap

topics.name: Effort Justification / Severe Initiation
topics.description: Valuing an outcome more highly because of the effort expended to obtain it, even when the effort itself added no objective value.

biases.name: Effort Justification
biases.description: After paying a meaningful effort cost to get something, people can value it more highly than the thing itself objectively warrants. Effort gets retrospectively rationalized into value.

topics.name: Ego Depletion & Self-Control
topics.description: The (contested) claim that self-control/willpower is a consumable resource that depletes with use across successive tasks.

biases.name: Ego Depletion
biases.description: The (contested) idea that self-control/willpower is a limited resource that depletes with use, making subsequent self-control tasks harder.

topics.name: Flow State (Challenge-Skill Balance)
topics.description: Whether a well-matched balance between task difficulty and user skill is the key driver of deep engagement — real, but only a moderate and non-dominant contributor once measured rigorously, contrary to how game/UX design discourse often treats it as the single lever.

biases.name: Flow
biases.description: A state of deep absorption where a task feels focused, controllable, and well matched to the person’s skill. In UX discussions, it is used to describe interfaces that help users stay immersed instead of getting knocked out by friction or confusion.

topics.name: Fresh Start Effect / Temporal Landmarks
topics.description: The finding that people are more likely to pursue goal-directed and aspirational behavior following a temporal landmark — New Year's Day, a birthday, a Monday — directly relevant to onboarding and goal-setting UX design timing.

biases.name: Fresh Start Effect
biases.description: Temporal landmarks like a new week, month, year, birthday, or return after a lapse can make people feel psychologically separated from past failures and more ready to begin again.

standalone_findings.description: Across 6 studies, salient temporal landmarks (e.g. a birthday) caused people to perceive their pre-landmark and post-landmark selves as more psychologically distinct and less connected -- the mechanism proposed to underlie the Fresh Start Effect, demonstrated by an independent research team using a different specific paradigm (self-continuity judgments, not archival search/gym/goal-commitment data). The landmark-induced discrepancy between one's current and desired future self increased motivation to pursue health/exercise goals and follow through on them, a direct behavioral outcome.
standalone_findings.source_title: The post-birthday world: Consequences of temporal landmarks for temporal self-appraisal and motivation
standalone_findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

topics.name: Goal Gradient Effect
topics.description: Effort and motivation increasing as a goal gets closer — directly behind loyalty-card, progress-bar, and 'almost there' design patterns, including the illusory-progress effect where a manufactured head start accelerates behavior even though the real remaining effort is unchanged.

biases.name: Goal Gradient Effect
biases.description: Effort and motivation toward a goal accelerate as perceived proximity to completion increases — including when that proximity is artificially pre-endowed rather than earned.

standalone_findings.description: A stronger individual tendency to accelerate effort as the goal approached predicted greater program retention and faster reengagement afterward — meaning the goal-gradient effect isn't just a short-term speed-up, it's associated with which customers stay engaged with a rewards program longer-term.
standalone_findings.source_title: The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention

standalone_findings.description: In an internet reward program where users rated songs for reward certificates, users visited the rating site more often, rated more songs per visit, and persisted longer in the effort as they approached the reward goal — the same acceleration pattern replicated in a digital-engagement context distinct from physical purchases.
standalone_findings.source_title: The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention

standalone_findings.description: Reframing an 8-step task as a 10-step task with 2 steps already artificially completed increased both the likelihood of task completion and decreased completion time, compared to the equivalent-effort 8-step task framed as not yet begun. The effect depends on perceived task completion progress rather than a desire to avoid wasting already-invested effort. This is the paper that named the phenomenon 'the endowed progress effect' -- the same alias already used for this corpus's BiasHeuristic entry.
standalone_findings.source_title: The Endowed Progress Effect: How Artificial Advancement Increases Effort

topics.name: Goal-Setting Theory (Specific & Difficult Goals)
topics.description: Locke & Latham's finding that specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than vague or easy goals — one of organizational psychology's most-cited applied theories, relevant to how products frame targets and milestones.

biases.name: Parkinson's Law
biases.description: Work expands to fill the time available for its completion.

standalone_findings.description: Reviewing 35 years of goal-setting research, Locke and Latham conclude that specific, difficult goals consistently produce higher task performance than vague ('do your best') or easy goals, an effect mediated by direction of attention, effort mobilization, persistence, and task-relevant strategy discovery, and moderated by factors including feedback, goal commitment, self-efficacy, and task complexity.
standalone_findings.source_title: Building a Practically Useful Theory of Goal Setting and Task Motivation: A 35-Year Odyssey

standalone_findings.description: Reviewing a program of experimental studies, Gollwitzer finds that supplementing a mere goal intention with a specific implementation intention (an if-then plan linking an anticipated situational cue to a concrete goal-directed response) substantially increases the likelihood that people actually initiate and complete the intended action, compared to holding the goal intention alone.
standalone_findings.source_title: Implementation Intentions: Strong Effects of Simple Plans

topics.name: Hot-Cold Empathy Gap
topics.description: People in a calm ('cold') state underestimate how much a visceral, emotionally 'hot' state will change their own future preferences and decisions, and vice versa.

biases.name: Empathy Gap
biases.description: People in one visceral or emotional state systematically mispredict what they will want, value, or choose in another state. Calm-state planning often fails to anticipate hot-state behavior, and hot-state choices can ignore what seemed sensible when calm.

standalone_findings.description: In a between-subject experiment manipulating appetite state (hungry vs. satiated) and consumption timing across virtual and real supermarket settings, de-Magistris, Lopez-Galan & Ballco found a genuine projection bias -- decisions made in one appetite state failed to fully account for the different appetite state at consumption time -- replicating in both virtual reality and a real supermarket, extending Fisher & Rangel's (2014) hot-cold valuation-gap bidding paradigm to naturalistic food-purchase decisions in a novel research modality.
standalone_findings.source_title: Do virtual reality experiments replicate projection bias phenomena? Examining the external validity of a virtual supermarket

topics.name: IKEA Effect / Labor-Leads-to-Love Valuation
topics.description: The finding that self-assembled or self-created products are valued more highly than equivalent pre-made ones — conditional on successful completion.

biases.name: IKEA Effect
biases.description: People who build/assemble a product themselves value it more highly than an equivalent pre-made product — but only if the build is completed successfully.

standalone_findings.description: A 3-study developmental series found the IKEA effect emerges at age 5, coinciding with self-concept formation milestones -- but neither the amount of effort invested (Study 2) nor feelings of ownership (Study 3) explained why children valued their own creations more, explicitly finding these results incompatible with existing theories of the IKEA bias (effort-justification and psychological-ownership accounts). Proposes instead that the effect reflects a link between one's creations and one's self-concept.
standalone_findings.source_title: When and how does labour lead to love? The ontogeny and mechanisms of the IKEA effect

standalone_findings.description: A direct conceptual replication of the original IKEA-effect willingness-to-pay paradigm confirmed the effect's robustness and identified psychological ownership as the underlying psychological mechanism.
standalone_findings.source_title: The IKEA Effect. A Conceptual Replication

standalone_findings.description: In a longitudinal study of 924 parent-child dyads, involving children in cooking activities increased their liking of vegetables and, mediated through that liking, their vegetable intake -- a real-world, public-health-relevant field application of the IKEA effect. The effect held for children specifically; involvement did not similarly predict parents' own vegetable liking or intake.
standalone_findings.source_title: Cooking together: The IKEA effect on family vegetable intake

topics.name: Implementation Intentions (If-Then Planning)
topics.description: Gollwitzer's 'if-then planning' research — specifying in advance when, where, and how you'll act on a goal substantially increases follow-through compared to just holding the goal, directly relevant to onboarding and habit-cue design.

biases.name: Implementation Intentions
biases.description: Forming a specific if-then plan that links an anticipated situational cue to a concrete intended action substantially increases the odds that the action actually gets initiated and completed, compared to holding only a general goal.

topics.name: Precommitment Devices
topics.description: The mechanism of voluntarily restricting one's own future choices to counteract predictable future self-control failure — distinct from Implementation Intentions, which is about if-then planning rather than binding future choice restriction.

biases.name: Precommitment Devices
biases.description: People will voluntarily adopt costly, binding constraints on their own future choices to counteract anticipated self-control failure (like procrastination), and doing so measurably improves outcomes relative to no constraint -- though self-chosen constraints tend to be less well-calibrated than equivalent externally-imposed ones.

topics.name: Present Bias & Hyperbolic Discounting
topics.description: Disproportionate weighting of immediate rewards/costs over future ones, and the discounting models (hyperbolic, quasi-hyperbolic) used to formalize it.

biases.name: Present Bias
biases.description: People place disproportionately high weight on immediate rewards/costs relative to future ones, leading to procrastination and undersaving.

biases.name: Restraint Bias
biases.description: People overestimate how well their future self will resist temptation or stay in control around triggers. Feeling strong now leads them to take exposure risks that make later self-control failures more likely.

standalone_findings.description: Across a field study (MIT executive-education students given the choice to self-impose grade-consequential deadlines for three papers) and follow-up lab studies, people voluntarily self-impose costly, binding deadlines to counteract their own anticipated procrastination, and doing so measurably improves task-completion timing and performance relative to no deadline at all -- but self-set deadlines are not optimally chosen for maximum performance and are less effective than deadlines of equivalent stringency imposed externally (evenly spaced deadlines set by the instructor outperformed self-chosen ones).
standalone_findings.source_title: Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment

topics.name: Restraint Bias / Illusion of Self-Restraint
topics.description: Overestimating one's own future ability to resist temptation or impulsive behavior.

biases.name: Restraint Bias
biases.description: People overestimate how well their future self will resist temptation or stay in control around triggers. Feeling strong now leads them to take exposure risks that make later self-control failures more likely.

topics.name: Route Familiarity & Travel-Time Estimation
topics.description: Familiar routes/tasks are judged as taking less time or effort than unfamiliar ones of genuinely equal length.

biases.name: Well-Traveled Road Effect
biases.description: Familiar routes can feel faster and easier than they really are, leading people to underestimate travel time or effort compared with unfamiliar paths. The popular label is sometimes broadened to familiar tasks too, but the clearest backing found here is specifically about route familiarity and travel-time judgment.

topics.name: Theoretical Domains Framework
topics.description: The Theoretical Domains Framework: a validated, 14-domain integrative classification of the theoretical constructs relevant to implementation and behavior-change research, used to diagnose which psychological/contextual barriers an intervention needs to address.

standalone_findings.description: Behavioural experts sorting 112 theoretical constructs provided good support for refining the Theoretical Domains Framework to 14 domains — Knowledge; Skills; Social/Professional Role and Identity; Beliefs about Capabilities; Optimism; Beliefs about Consequences; Reinforcement; Intentions; Goals; Memory, Attention and Decision Processes; Environmental Context and Resources; Social Influences; Emotions; and Behavioural Regulation — with an average silhouette value of 0.29. The authors conclude the refined TDF provides a strengthened theoretical basis for assessing implementation problems and health-related behaviours before designing interventions.
standalone_findings.source_title: Validation of the theoretical domains framework for use in behaviour change and implementation research

topics.name: Time-Saving Bias
topics.description: Misjudging the time saved by increasing speed: people underestimate time saved moving from slow to moderate speeds, and overestimate savings moving from fast to very fast speeds.

biases.name: Time-Saving Bias
biases.description: People misjudge how much time a speed increase will actually save. We intuitively undervalue moving from slow to moderately faster speeds and overvalue squeezing a little extra speed out of an already fast process.

topics.name: Context-Dependent Habit Cues
topics.description: How environmental and contextual cues trigger automatic behavior, distinct from how long a habit takes to form — why changing an app's layout or a routine's setting disrupts habitual usage even when the underlying behavior hasn't changed.

standalone_findings.description: Everyday habits (exercise, newspaper reading, TV watching) among students transferring to a new university persisted after the move only when key features of the performance context stayed stable (e.g., same co-present others); when the context changed, habit performance was disrupted and behavior came back under the control of current intentions — changes in intentions alone did not explain the disruption.
standalone_findings.source_title: Changing circumstances, disrupting habits
standalone_findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

standalone_findings.description: Habits are proposed to form through the gradual learning of associations between a response and the recurring features of the context in which it was performed (e.g., physical setting, preceding action); once formed, mere perception of the associated context triggers the response directly, without goals mediating the link — meaning habitual automaticity is bound to the recurrence of the triggering context, not simply to elapsed practice time or motivation.
standalone_findings.source_title: A new look at habits and the habit-goal interface

standalone_findings.description: In an experience-sampling study of daily behavior, habitual actions were more reliably predicted by stable contextual cues (physical location, the immediately preceding action in a sequence) than by people's own verbal reports of what triggered the behavior, indicating people have limited conscious awareness of the specific environmental cues actually driving their habitual behavior.
standalone_findings.source_title: How do habits guide behavior? Perceived and actual triggers of habits in daily life

topics.name: Gamification Effectiveness
topics.description: Whether game-like mechanics (points, badges, progress, competition) actually improve motivation and engagement in non-game products — the applied synthesis of reinforcement-schedule and overjustification research, with real effects that are genuinely context- and user-dependent rather than guaranteed.

biases.name: Gamification
biases.description: Adding game-like mechanics such as points, badges, streaks, or leaderboards can improve motivation and behavior, but the effect is highly context- and user-dependent rather than automatic.

topics.name: Habit Formation
topics.description: How long and how reliably a repeated behavior becomes automatic — the popularized '66 days' figure is a real study's average masking an enormous range (18 to 254 days), directly relevant to any onboarding/streak design that assumes a fixed habit-formation timeline.

standalone_findings.description: Modeling daily habit-formation data from 96 volunteers over 12 weeks found automaticity increased along an asymptotic curve, reaching 95% of its ceiling after an average of 66 days — but with enormous individual variation, ranging from 18 to 254 days. Missing a single opportunity to perform the behavior did not meaningfully disrupt the process. The popularized '66 days to form a habit' claim is the average of a distribution wide enough that some people took over 8 months.
standalone_findings.effect_size: 18–254 days to reach 95% of automaticity ceiling, mean ≈ 66 days
standalone_findings.source_title: How Are Habits Formed: Modelling Habit Formation in the Real World

topics.name: Reinforcement Schedules & Superstitious Learning
topics.description: How intermittent, non-contingent reward delivery produces persistent, repeated behavior — the mechanism popularly invoked to explain compulsive app-checking and notification-driven habits, and a real dispute over whether Skinner's 'accidental reinforcement' account or an antecedent-stimulus account better explains it.

biases.name: Superstitious Conditioning
biases.description: Behavior that happens to occur just before a reward is delivered, even when the reward is actually independent of that behavior, can get strengthened and repeated through pure accidental timing -- though a later, larger review finds this classic mechanism is weaker and less well-supported than commonly assumed.

topics.name: Unit Bias
topics.description: A preference for consuming or completing one whole 'unit' of something (a portion, a task), largely independent of that unit's actual size.

biases.name: Unit Bias
biases.description: People often treat one whole unit of something as the natural or appropriate amount, even when the unit size is arbitrary. Finishing one portion, one scoop, or one packaged chunk can feel right regardless of its actual size.

topics.name: Variable-Ratio Reinforcement & Persistent Engagement
topics.description: Why unpredictable, intermittent rewards produce the highest, most extinction-resistant response rates — the actual mechanism behind slot machines, notification-checking, and pull-to-refresh engagement loops, distinct from the accidental/non-contingent reinforcement covered under Reinforcement Schedules.

biases.name: Variable-Ratio Reinforcement
biases.description: Rewarding a behavior after an unpredictable number of responses, rather than a fixed number or fixed interval, produces high and steady response rates with minimal pausing after reward, and makes the behavior markedly more resistant to extinction than behavior reinforced on a continuous or fixed schedule.

standalone_findings.description: The intermittent, variable, unpredictable timing of smartphone notifications functions as a variable-ratio-like reward schedule: a cue-reward pairing that resolves around a 50% delivery rate is theorized to be maximally 'enticing but anxiety-inducing' (more arousing than a highly predictable low- or high-probability schedule), which the authors propose drives compulsive checking behavior via social-reward anticipation and prediction-error mechanisms.
standalone_findings.source_title: Hypernatural Monitoring: A Social Rehearsal Account of Smartphone Addiction

domains.name: Intrinsic Motivation & Well-Being
domains.description: The quality of motivation and its link to well-being, distinct from whether a goal gets pursued at all.

topics.name: Hedonic Adaptation & Affective Forecasting (Impact Bias)
topics.description: People are systematically bad at predicting how happy or unhappy future events will make them (affective forecasting/impact bias), and tend to adapt back to an emotional baseline faster than expected — relevant to how products set expectations about outcomes.

biases.name: Focusing Effect
biases.description: When judging a complex outcome, people overweight the salient feature currently in view and neglect the rest of what will matter in real life. What is easy to think about temporarily feels more important than it really is.

biases.name: Hedonic Adaptation / Impact Bias
biases.description: People adapt faster than expected to positive and negative experiences, and they also mispredict how intense or lasting those feelings will be. New features, rewards, or setbacks rarely feel as transformative for as long as teams or users expect.

standalone_findings.description: Kim & Oswald identify a previously unrecognized methodological weakness (lottery-ticket bias -- unobservable variation in how much people spend on lottery tickets) that had masked lottery windfalls' true effect on happiness in prior research including Brickman et al.'s 1978 study. Correcting for this bias in a large Singapore sample (n=5,626), they find lottery windfalls DO predict substantial improvements in happiness and well-being -- directly disputing the original small-sample finding that lottery winners were no happier than controls.
standalone_findings.source_title: Happy Lottery Winners and Lottery-Ticket Bias

topics.name: Overjustification Effect (Extrinsic Rewards vs. Intrinsic Motivation)
topics.description: Whether adding an explicit extrinsic reward for something people already enjoy doing undermines their intrinsic motivation to keep doing it once the reward is gone — directly relevant to any design pattern layering badges, points, or streaks onto an activity, with a real nuance: positive feedback alone behaves in the opposite direction.

biases.name: Overjustification Effect
biases.description: When people already enjoy an activity, adding a salient external reward can reduce their intrinsic motivation to keep doing it once the reward disappears. Extrinsic incentives can crowd out the internal reason for acting.

topics.name: Self-Determination Theory (Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness)
topics.description: The theory that autonomy, competence, and relatedness are basic psychological needs driving intrinsic motivation — the broader framework behind the overjustification effect, now including its direct application to digital product and game design (the METUX model).

biases.name: User Control and Freedom
biases.description: Users should be able to back out, undo, cancel, or leave unwanted states without feeling trapped. Recoverability matters as much as initial correctness.

standalone_findings.description: Across a systematic review of 110 CHI/CHI PLAY papers citing SDT, the needs for competence and autonomy (and, less consistently, relatedness) are widely used to analyze player experience and inform game/UX design, but most HCI papers engage with SDT only descriptively — applying its needs constructs and measures without engaging its deeper theoretical propositions or mini-theories, leaving conceptual gaps in how rigorously SDT is actually being tested in digital-product contexts.
standalone_findings.source_title: Self-Determination Theory in HCI Games Research: Current Uses and Open Questions
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the 2020 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems

standalone_findings.description: Self-Determination Theory holds that psychological growth, integrity, and wellbeing depend on satisfaction of three innate psychological needs — autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Social contexts that support these needs facilitate intrinsically motivated behavior and healthy integration of extrinsic motivation; contexts that thwart any of the three are associated with poorer motivation, performance, and wellbeing.
standalone_findings.source_title: The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior

standalone_findings.description: The METUX (Motivation, Engagement and Thriving in User Experience) model argues that technology designs support or undermine user motivation, engagement, and wellbeing to the extent they satisfy the SDT needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness — and that this needs-satisfaction analysis should be applied across six spheres: technology adoption, interface interaction, task engagement, technology-supported behavior, overall life, and society.
standalone_findings.source_title: Designing for Motivation, Engagement and Wellbeing in Digital Experience

topics.name: Cognitive Load Theory
topics.description: The theory that working memory has limited capacity, and that exceeding it during a task impairs learning/performance — the foundational basis for 'simplify the interface' design guidance, and the real open questions about how cognitive load is actually measured.

biases.name: Cognitive Load
biases.description: The amount of mental effort required to understand what an interface is saying and how to use it. Interfaces feel harder when they force users to hold, compare, or interpret more than working memory comfortably supports.

standalone_findings.description: A critical review identifies significant open conceptual, methodological, and application-related problems in cognitive load theory as commonly used — most centrally, that 'cognitive load' itself has no single agreed, validated measurement approach (self-report, physiological, and performance-based measures often disagree), which undermines confident claims that a specific design intervention actually reduced cognitive load rather than just being assumed to.
standalone_findings.source_title: Cognitive Load Theory, Educational Research, and Instructional Design: Some Food for Thought

topics.name: Confabulation
topics.description: Unintentionally fabricating a false but subjectively believed memory or explanation to fill a gap, without any intent to deceive.

biases.name: Confabulation
biases.description: When memory or explanation is missing, people may sincerely produce false accounts without intending to deceive. The invented story feels subjectively true to the person telling it.

topics.name: Context-Dependent Memory
topics.description: Memory retrieval is easier when the physical or mental context at recall matches the context present during original encoding.

biases.name: Context Effect
biases.description: Memory retrieval improves when the cues present at recall match the environment or context in which information was learned. What people remember is partly shaped by where and under what conditions they encoded it, not just by the content itself.

biases.name: Cue-Dependent Forgetting
biases.description: People can fail to retrieve information not because it is gone, but because the cue available at recall does not match the cue under which it was encoded. Memory often looks lost when the route back into it is missing.

topics.name: Cue-Dependent Forgetting / Encoding Specificity
topics.description: Memory retrieval fails when the specific cues present during original encoding are absent at the moment of retrieval — the encoding-specificity principle underlying much of forgetting.

biases.name: Cue-Dependent Forgetting
biases.description: People can fail to retrieve information not because it is gone, but because the cue available at recall does not match the cue under which it was encoded. Memory often looks lost when the route back into it is missing.

topics.name: Digital Transactive Memory / Search-Engine Memory
topics.description: Knowing that information is easily searchable online reduces the tendency to internally memorize that information — a 'digital amnesia' or transactive-memory effect directly relevant to search/reminder product design.

biases.name: Google Effect
biases.description: When people expect information to stay easily searchable online, they tend to remember the information itself less and remember the route back to it more. The mind offloads content memory toward location or access memory when retrieval feels cheap.

topics.name: Fading Affect Bias
topics.description: The negative emotion originally associated with a memory fades faster over time than the positive emotion associated with it.

biases.name: Fading Affect Bias
biases.description: The emotional sting of negative autobiographical memories tends to fade faster over time than the positive feeling attached to good memories. As time passes, the remembered emotional balance of the past can drift upward.

topics.name: False Memory
topics.description: A person remembers an event that did not actually occur, or remembers a real event in a substantially altered way, while genuinely believing the memory is accurate.

biases.name: False Memory
biases.description: People can remember events or details that never happened, or remember them in materially distorted form. False memories can arise from suggestion, associative lure, imagination, or source confusion rather than deliberate lying.

topics.name: Generation Effect / Self-Generated Learning
topics.description: Information is remembered better when a person actively generates it themselves rather than simply reading or receiving it passively.

biases.name: Generation Effect
biases.description: Information is usually remembered better when people generate it themselves than when they only read or receive it passively. Producing the answer, label, or completion tends to create a stronger memory trace than merely seeing it.

topics.name: Humor and Memory
topics.description: Humorous or incongruous material is remembered better than comparable non-humorous material, likely via added distinctiveness/processing.

biases.name: Humor Effect
biases.description: Humorous material is often remembered better than equivalent nonhumorous material. The effect is about memorability, not a blanket claim that humorous interfaces are always better or more usable.

topics.name: Interrupted-Task Memory & Resumption (Zeigarnik/Ovsiankina Effects)
