topics.description: Whether interrupted/incomplete tasks are remembered better than completed ones (the popular 'Zeigarnik effect' claim behind progress bars and 'continue where you left off' prompts), and the distinct, better-supported tendency to want to resume an interrupted task (the Ovsiankina effect) that the memory claim is often conflated with.

biases.name: Zeigarnik Effect
biases.description: Interrupted or unfinished tasks tend to stay mentally active and keep pulling for closure. In design practice this is often framed as a memory effect, but the better-supported part is the urge to resume and complete the open task.

standalone_findings.description: Zeigarnik's original 1927 dissertation research reported that interrupted, incomplete tasks were remembered significantly better than completed ones — the origin of the popular 'Zeigarnik effect' claim widely invoked in design practice (progress bars, 'continue where you left off' prompts, cliffhangers).
standalone_findings.source_title: Zeigarnik and von Restorff: The Memory Effects and the Stories Behind Them

topics.name: Leveling and Sharpening
topics.description: Over repeated retelling, memories tend to be simplified/leveled (details dropped) or selectively emphasized/sharpened (particular details exaggerated).

biases.name: Leveling and Sharpening
biases.description: As stories are retold, some details are flattened or dropped ('leveling') while a few striking or schema-fitting details get exaggerated ('sharpening'). Repetition does not preserve memory neutrally; it edits it.

topics.name: Levels / Depth of Processing
topics.description: Deeper, more meaningful processing during encoding (e.g. semantic processing) produces better later memory than shallow processing (e.g. surface/perceptual features).

biases.name: Levels of Processing Effect
biases.description: Information processed for meaning is remembered better later than information processed only for shallow surface features. The way something is encoded matters at least as much as how often it was merely seen.

topics.name: Memory Distinctiveness & Isolation Effects
topics.description: Why an item that stands out from surrounding similar items is remembered better, and the more nuanced mechanism behind that effect than the popular 'stand out visually' shorthand implies.

biases.name: Bizarreness Effect
biases.description: Unusual, bizarre, or incongruous material can be remembered better than ordinary material, especially when its distinctiveness stands out against a more normal surrounding context. The memorability comes from relative distinctiveness, not from 'weirdness' as a universal design virtue.

biases.name: Von Restorff Effect
biases.description: An item that stands out from surrounding similar items is remembered better than the others.

topics.name: Memory Misattribution / Source Monitoring
topics.description: A memory, or its source, gets attributed to the wrong origin — including mistaking a forgotten prior exposure for an original idea (cryptomnesia) or misremembering where/how information was learned.

biases.name: Cryptomnesia
biases.description: A person mistakes a forgotten prior exposure for a brand-new idea of their own. Something retrieved from memory is experienced as originality because its source has been lost.

biases.name: Memory Misattribution
biases.description: People can remember content yet misremember where it came from — whether it was perceived, imagined, suggested by someone else, or encountered in another context. The memory feels real, but its source tag is wrong.

topics.name: Mere Exposure Effect
topics.description: Whether repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking for it with no reward or conscious evaluation required — the psychology behind familiar-pattern and repeated-branding arguments in design, and its real boundary condition (satiation/boredom at very high exposure counts).

biases.name: Mere Exposure Effect
biases.description: Repeated exposure to a stimulus can increase liking or preference even without reward or deeper evaluation. Familiarity itself can make a design, message, or brand element feel better.

standalone_findings.description: The exposure-liking relationship is not linear without limit: it follows an inverted-U shape, and very high numbers of exposures can trigger satiation/boredom that reduces or reverses the effect — a real boundary condition against a naive 'more repetition is always better' reading, directly relevant to how often a design pattern/brand element should actually be repeated.
standalone_findings.source_title: Exposure and Affect: Overview and Meta-Analysis of Research, 1968-1987

topics.name: Mood-Congruent Memory
topics.description: Memories that match a person's current mood are recalled more easily than memories that don't match it.

biases.name: Mood-Congruent Memory
biases.description: People more easily retrieve memories whose emotional tone matches their current mood. A sad mood can make negative material come to mind more readily, while a positive mood can surface more positive recollections.

topics.name: Part-List Cuing / Cueing Effect
topics.description: Providing some items from a list as retrieval cues can actually impair recall of the remaining, non-cued items.

biases.name: Part-List Cueing Effect
biases.description: Giving people some items from a studied list as retrieval cues can make the remaining items harder to recall. Partial help can interfere with a person's own retrieval strategy instead of improving it.

topics.name: Picture Superiority Effect
topics.description: Pictures are recalled and recognized more reliably than the equivalent information presented as words alone.

biases.name: Picture Superiority Effect
biases.description: Pictures are typically remembered better than equivalent verbal material. Visual representations can leave a stronger memory trace than text alone, especially when they provide an additional code or cue for retrieval.

standalone_findings.description: Free recall of pictures was better than free recall of words (Experiment 1), directly confirming the standard picture-superiority pattern in the same paradigm as Paivio & Csapo's original demonstration. However, on an implicit word-fragment-completion memory test, words produced GREATER priming than pictures -- reversing the typical superiority pattern. Across 4 experiments, the type of retrieval test (not just the study format) determines whether pictures or words show superior retention, consistent with transfer-appropriate processing.
standalone_findings.source_title: Altering retrieval demands reverses the picture superiority effect

topics.name: Recognition vs. Recall
topics.description: Why recognizing something already encountered is a fundamentally easier memory task than recalling it unprompted — the empirical basis for Nielsen's 'recognition rather than recall' usability heuristic (menus and visible options over remembered commands).

biases.name: Recognition Rather Than Recall
biases.description: Interfaces should make actions, options, and information visible enough that users can recognize what they need instead of having to remember it from memory. Recognition is cognitively easier than unaided recall, especially in repeated product use.

biases.name: Tip of the Tongue Phenomenon
biases.description: A person can feel sure they know a word or name yet be temporarily unable to retrieve it. During the state, partial information often remains available, such as the first letter, syllable pattern, or semantically related alternatives.

topics.name: Retrieval-Induced Forgetting / Memory Inhibition
topics.description: Actively retrieving certain memories can suppress later recall of related-but-not-retrieved memories.

biases.name: Memory Inhibition
biases.description: Retrieving some memories can make related competing memories harder to recall later. Remembering is not only strengthening; it can also suppress neighboring traces.

topics.name: Rosy Retrospection / Rosy View
topics.description: Remembering a past experience as more positive than it was actually rated at the time it occurred.

biases.name: Rosy Retrospection
biases.description: People often remember past experiences as better than they felt in the moment. Memory polishes the past, so the remembered version can become more positive than the live experience actually was.

standalone_findings.description: Using smartphone-based Ecological Momentary Assessment (n=92) to compare momentary and later-recalled daily affect, Colombo et al. independently confirm the same retrospective-more-positive-than-real-time mechanism Mitchell et al. identified, and additionally find positive-affect overestimation is associated with better mental health, higher well-being, and lower depression/anxiety symptoms -- a genuine extension linking the rosy-retrospection mechanism to psychological resilience, not present in the original study.
standalone_findings.source_title: Affect Recall Bias: Being Resilient by Distorting Reality

topics.name: Self-Reference / Self-Relevance Effect
topics.description: Information framed as relevant to oneself is processed more deeply and remembered better than equivalent non-self-referential information.

biases.name: Self-Relevance Effect
biases.description: Information tied to the self is remembered better than otherwise similar information processed in less self-related ways. Asking people to connect material to their own goals, identity, or circumstances often makes it stick.

topics.name: Serial Position Effects in Memory
topics.description: Why items at the start and end of a sequence are recalled better than items in the middle.

biases.name: Modality Effect
biases.description: Immediate recall can change depending on whether information was heard or seen. In the classic list-memory version, spoken items often get an end-of-list memory advantage relative to visually presented items.

biases.name: Next-in-Line Effect
biases.description: People often remember less of what happened immediately before their own turn to speak or perform. Anticipating one's upcoming turn can pull attention inward, so the just-preceding material never gets encoded well in the first place.

biases.name: Serial Position Effect
biases.description: Items at the beginning and end of a list/sequence are remembered better than items in the middle.

biases.name: Suffix Effect
biases.description: Adding an irrelevant final item after a list can selectively damage memory for the true last items. The extra ending element disrupts the normal recency advantage those items would otherwise have.

topics.name: Spacing Effect (Distributed vs. Massed Practice)
topics.description: Whether spreading study/practice sessions out over time produces better long-term retention than massing them together — a large, well-established meta-analytic literature directly relevant to spaced-repetition and onboarding-pacing design.

biases.name: Spacing Effect
biases.description: Information practiced or revisited over spaced intervals is remembered better than the same practice massed together. The best spacing depends on how long the material needs to stick.

topics.name: Telescoping Effect / Temporal Misdating
topics.description: Misremembering when an event happened: recent events feel more distant than they were, and distant events feel more recent.

biases.name: Telescoping Effect
biases.description: People can misremember when an event happened, pulling distant events forward or pushing recent events backward relative to their true date. The event is remembered, but its position in time is reconstructed inaccurately.

topics.name: Testing Effect / Retrieval Practice
topics.description: Whether actively retrieving information from memory (quizzing, self-testing) produces better retention than passive re-study — directly relevant to how tutorials and learning products should be structured, confirmed by both a founding study and a later meta-analysis.

biases.name: Generation Effect
biases.description: Information is usually remembered better when people generate it themselves than when they only read or receive it passively. Producing the answer, label, or completion tends to create a stronger memory trace than merely seeing it.

biases.name: Testing Effect
biases.description: People remember information better when they have to actively retrieve it than when they only re-read it. In interface terms, doing and recalling usually teaches better than passively seeing the same thing again.

topics.name: Working Memory Capacity
topics.description: How many discrete items of information short-term/working memory can hold at once, and how that estimate has been revised over time.

biases.name: Chunking
biases.description: Grouping related pieces of information into meaningful units so people can scan, hold, and work with them more easily. In interface design, chunking turns an undifferentiated wall of options or content into manageable parts.

biases.name: List-Length Effect
biases.description: As lists get longer, people typically remember a smaller share of the items. Longer sequences dilute rehearsal and make later recall less reliable, even if the absolute number remembered does not always drop in lockstep.

biases.name: Miller's Law
biases.description: Human working memory reliably holds around 7 (plus or minus 2) discrete chunks of information at once.

domains.name: Motor & Interaction Mechanics
domains.description: The mechanics of physically operating an interface.

topics.name: Automation Bias
topics.description: Over-trusting automated or algorithmic recommendations over one's own independent judgment, including failing to notice when the automation is wrong — directly relevant to AI-assisted feature design.

biases.name: Automation Bias
biases.description: People can overweight automated recommendations and fail to adequately check them, even when the system is fallible. The result is both accepting wrong machine advice and missing problems the system failed to flag.

topics.name: Choice Reaction Time (Hick's Law)
topics.description: How the number of available choices/response alternatives affects decision speed (Hick's Law), including its documented boundary conditions.

biases.name: Hick's Law
biases.description: The time to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices available.

topics.name: Error Prevention Through System & Interaction Design
topics.description: How system and interaction design (decision support, confirmation prompts, automated reminders, human-review layers) actually prevents real errors before they reach a user — grounded in patient-safety/clinical-informatics research, the domain with the clearest, most rigorously measured evidence for this design principle.

biases.name: Error Prevention
biases.description: It is better to stop an error from being possible, or make it hard, than to rely on a good error message afterward. Good design removes traps before recovery is needed.

topics.name: Mental Models
topics.description: The compressed, often incomplete internal representations people build of how a system works, used to predict its behavior and guide interaction — an interdisciplinary construct spanning cognitive science, environmental management, and design.

biases.name: Consistency and Standards
biases.description: Users should not have to relearn the same thing on each screen; repeated patterns, terminology, and platform conventions should mean the same thing each time.

biases.name: Jakob's Law
biases.description: Users spend most of their time on other sites/products, so they prefer yours to work the way those already do.

biases.name: Match Between System and the Real World
biases.description: Interfaces should present concepts, language, and ordering in terms users already understand rather than internal system logic. The goal is not literal skeuomorphism but conceptual fit with the user's world.

biases.name: Mental Model
biases.description: The internal picture a person has of how a system works and what will happen when they act. Designers rely on mental models when they reuse familiar patterns so users can predict behavior without relearning everything from scratch.

biases.name: Tesler's Law
biases.description: For any system, there is a certain amount of complexity that cannot be reduced — it can only be moved between the user and the system/developer.

standalone_findings.description: In human-AI decision-making teams, a human's mental model of the AI system's error boundary (knowing when the AI is likely to be wrong) is a key factor in team performance, beyond the AI's raw accuracy -- it determines whether the human correctly accepts or overrides the AI's recommendation. Experimentally manipulated properties of the AI's error boundary (parsimony, stochasticity) and task dimensionality were shown to affect how accurately humans form this mental model, and consequently, team performance. Directly design-relevant to AI-feature interfaces: how an AI system communicates its own limitations shapes whether users build an accurate mental model of it.
standalone_findings.source_title: Beyond Accuracy: The Role of Mental Models in Human-AI Team Performance
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Human Computation and Crowdsourcing

topics.name: Micro-Interactions & Feedback-Loop Design
topics.description: How small, immediate UI feedback — button states, loading micro-animations, action confirmation — affects perceived responsiveness and user confidence. The thinnest-sourced topic in the corpus as of 2026-09-01: only one modern empirical study exists, alongside the much older but foundational progress-indicator research.

biases.name: Visibility of System Status
biases.description: Interfaces should keep users informed about what the system is doing, especially after an action or during waiting. Visible status reduces guessing and makes latency or background work feel accountable.

standalone_findings.description: In a between-subjects experiment (n=49), a smartphone app prototype with micro-interaction animations produced a numerically higher mean System Usability Scale (SUS) score than an otherwise identical prototype without them, but a Wilcoxon test found this overall SUS difference was NOT statistically significant. Specific subjective survey items (interestingness, likeability, pleasantness) were rated more positively for the micro-interaction version. This is a genuinely mixed result — it does not support a strong claim that micro-interactions measurably improve overall perceived usability, only that they may shift specific affective/subjective impressions, in a single small unreplicated study.
standalone_findings.source_title: Can micro interactions in user interfaces affect their perceived usability?
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the 32nd European Conference on Cognitive Ergonomics (ECCE 2021)

standalone_findings.description: The same experiment attempted to replicate an earlier published claim that users prefer constant over variable response times, and that this preference reverses in the presence of a progress indicator. This replication attempt was NOT statistically significant — the study found no significant preference for constant response time at all, contradicting the earlier published results it was designed to replicate. Included as an early, honest example of a specific mechanistic sub-claim in this space failing to replicate, within the same paper that produced the well-replicated general preference finding above.
standalone_findings.source_title: The importance of percent-done progress indicators for computer-human interfaces
standalone_findings.source_venue: ACM SIGCHI Bulletin (Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, CHI '85)

topics.name: Motor Control & Target Acquisition (Fitts's Law)
topics.description: The relationship between a UI target's size/distance and how long it takes to accurately select it (Fitts's Law).

biases.name: Fitts's Law
biases.description: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to it and its size — smaller, more distant targets take longer to hit accurately.

standalone_findings.description: A review of 24 published Fitts' law models applied to mouse-pointing tasks (spanning 1978-2004) plus 9 independent studies using the 2002 ISO 9241-9 pointing-device evaluation standard confirms the law's broad empirical generalization well beyond Fitts's original 1954 motor-control experiments -- citing prior work (Plamondon & Alimi, 1997) documenting the effect across serial tapping, dial rotation, and object-transfer tasks; multiple body parts (fingers, hands, arms, feet, head, eyes); varied physical conditions (including underwater and under a microscope); and diverse populations (young, aged, motor-impaired). At the same time, the review identifies a genuine methodological problem across this same literature: inconsistent mathematical formulations and throughput-calculation methods since Fitts' law's 1978 introduction to HCI research have made many published results not directly comparable across studies -- the reason the ISO 9241-9 standard was created in 2002, and the motivation for this paper's own seven standardization recommendations.
standalone_findings.source_title: Towards a standard for pointing device evaluation, perspectives on 27 years of Fitts' law research in HCI

standalone_findings.description: An independent experiment testing Fitts' law's original one-dimensional formulation against two-dimensional (rectangular) on-screen targets found the naive model can break down, producing unrealistically low or even negative index-of-difficulty ratings for certain target shapes -- but that the Shannon formulation of Fitts' law (already an established variant, not new to this paper) substantially corrects the problem, and that redefining "target width" for the 2D case further improves the model's predictive accuracy, confirmed experimentally.
standalone_findings.source_title: Extending Fitts' law to two-dimensional tasks
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '92)

topics.name: Novice-to-Expert Transitions in User Interfaces
topics.description: How user interfaces can support a user's gradual shift from novice to expert operation (e.g. progressive disclosure, shortcuts alongside guided flows) without forcing a hard choice between the two.

biases.name: Flexibility and Efficiency of Use
biases.description: Interfaces should work for novices while also enabling faster, higher-throughput use as expertise grows, often through shortcuts, customization, or accelerators. The key design problem is supporting the transition to expert use, not just adding power-user features and hoping they are discovered.

topics.name: Paradox of the Active User
topics.description: Why people learning new software start doing rather than read comprehensive instructions first — the empirical basis for short, task-focused, error-recovery-oriented documentation and onboarding design outperforming exhaustive manuals.

biases.name: Help Users Recognize, Diagnose, and Recover from Errors
biases.description: When users hit a problem, the interface should explain it in plain language and make the path to recovery obvious. The goal is not merely surfacing an error state, but helping people understand what went wrong and recover without getting stuck.

biases.name: Help and Documentation
biases.description: Even highly usable products sometimes need help content; good documentation is easy to search, focused on concrete tasks, concise, and available at the moment of need rather than assuming users will read a manual front to back.

topics.name: System Response Time & Productivity
topics.description: How quickly a system responds to user input, and its measured effect on productivity and subjective satisfaction — the empirical basis behind the Doherty Threshold's sub-second-response claim.

biases.name: Doherty Threshold
biases.description: People stay more engaged and productive when an interactive system responds quickly enough that waiting does not break their train of thought. In design practice, this is usually summarized as keeping response times under roughly 400 ms.

standalone_findings.description: A 40-year literature review of system response time research concludes there is no single universal response-time cutoff. Instead, interactions split into 'control tasks' (requiring immediate response for optimal performance) and 'conversational tasks' (where some delay can be tolerated, or even help maintain pacing) -- the appropriate response-time threshold depends on task complexity and user expectations rather than one fixed number like the popularly-cited '400 milliseconds.'
standalone_findings.source_title: 40 years of searching for the best computer system response time

domains.name: Probability & Value Judgment
domains.description: How people estimate frequency, probability, and value, and the systematic errors in that estimation.

topics.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
topics.description: The finding that users perceive more visually appealing interfaces as more usable even when actual usability is held constant — the 'what is beautiful is usable' effect, and how reliably it replicates across different samples and study designs.

biases.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
biases.description: Visually appealing designs are often perceived as easier to use, and can genuinely improve task performance under certain conditions.

topics.name: Affect Heuristic
topics.description: Whether people derive both risk and benefit judgments from a single underlying emotional reaction to something, rather than evaluating each independently — directly relevant to how visual/emotional design choices shape perceived trust and safety.

biases.name: Affect Heuristic
biases.description: People often use an overall gut feeling to judge risks and benefits, letting a single affective impression stand in for more deliberate analysis. Things that feel good are judged as more beneficial and less risky, and vice versa.

topics.name: Ambiguity Aversion / Ellsberg Paradox
topics.description: A preference for known-probability risks over same-expected-value but ambiguous/unknown-probability options — the Ellsberg paradox's violation of standard expected-utility theory.

biases.name: Ambiguity Bias
biases.description: Given a choice, people often prefer options with known odds over comparable options whose probabilities are unclear or hard to estimate. Uncertainty about the distribution itself feels aversive, not just uncertainty about the outcome.

topics.name: Anchoring Effects
topics.description: How exposure to an initial number or value skews subsequent judgments and valuations, even when that anchor is arbitrary.

biases.name: Anchoring Bias
biases.description: Initial exposure to a number or value ('anchor') skews subsequent judgments and valuations toward that anchor, even when the anchor is arbitrary or irrelevant.

topics.name: Anecdotal Fallacy / Vivid Anecdotes Over Statistics
topics.description: Generalizing from a small number of vivid personal anecdotes in preference to more representative but less vivid statistical evidence.

biases.name: Anecdotal Fallacy
biases.description: A vivid personal story can outweigh broader statistical evidence, leading people to generalize from one memorable case instead of the larger pattern. Concrete anecdotes feel more diagnostic than pallid summaries.

topics.name: Availability Heuristic
topics.description: Tversky & Kahneman's foundational finding that people judge the frequency or probability of an event by how easily examples come to mind, rather than by actual base rates.

biases.name: Anecdotal Fallacy
biases.description: A vivid personal story can outweigh broader statistical evidence, leading people to generalize from one memorable case instead of the larger pattern. Concrete anecdotes feel more diagnostic than pallid summaries.

biases.name: Availability Heuristic
biases.description: People judge what is likely, frequent, or important by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent, or memorable cases therefore feel more common than they really are.

biases.name: Frequency Illusion
biases.description: After noticing something once, people can feel as if it suddenly appears everywhere. The experience is usually described as a mix of selective noticing and biased interpretation of subsequent encounters rather than a settled standalone experimental law.

topics.name: Base Rate Neglect / Base Rate Fallacy
topics.description: The tendency to underweight general statistical base-rate information in favor of vivid, specific case information when making probability judgments — one of the original Kahneman & Tversky heuristics-and-biases findings.

biases.name: Anecdotal Fallacy
biases.description: A vivid personal story can outweigh broader statistical evidence, leading people to generalize from one memorable case instead of the larger pattern. Concrete anecdotes feel more diagnostic than pallid summaries.

biases.name: Base Rate Fallacy
biases.description: People often underweight general statistical base-rate information when a vivid or representative case description is available, letting the specific story dominate the probabilities.

topics.name: Belief Bias
topics.description: Judging an argument's logical validity based on how believable its conclusion is, rather than on the argument's actual logical structure.

biases.name: Belief Bias
biases.description: People can judge an argument as logically stronger when its conclusion sounds believable, and weaker when its conclusion sounds implausible, even if the formal logic says otherwise. Plausibility leaks into validity judgment.

standalone_findings.description: Trippas, Kellen, Singmann, Pennycook, Koehler, Fugelsang & Dube's hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of 22 confidence-rating studies (N=993) resolves the Dube et al. (2010) signal-detection-artifact critique that had called belief bias into question: using appropriate hierarchical measurement methods, belief bias is confirmed as a genuine phenomenon in syllogistic reasoning, moderated by individual differences and task format rather than being a measurement artifact.
standalone_findings.source_title: Characterizing belief bias in syllogistic reasoning: A hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of ROC data

topics.name: Belief Updating / Bayesian Conservatism
topics.description: How readily people revise a belief in light of new evidence relative to an ideal (Bayesian) updating rule — conservatism describes systematic under-updating relative to that ideal.

biases.name: Conservatism Bias
biases.description: People revise beliefs in the direction of new evidence, but not far enough. They stay too attached to prior assumptions relative to what a Bayesian update would imply.

topics.name: Choice Blindness
topics.description: Whether people notice when the outcome of their own stated choice or preference is covertly swapped — they mostly don't, and will often confabulate reasons for a choice they never actually made. Directly relevant to how much weight self-reported preference data in user research and survey validation actually deserves.

biases.name: Choice Blindness
biases.description: People frequently fail to notice when the outcome of their own choice is covertly swapped for the option they rejected, and will go on to confidently construct coherent reasons defending a preference they never actually held -- a direct challenge to the reliability of introspective self-report about one's own preferences and reasons.

topics.name: Clustering Illusion
topics.description: Perceiving meaningful clusters or streaks in what is actually random data, because truly random sequences don't look 'random' to intuition.

biases.name: Clustering Illusion
biases.description: People see meaningful streaks, hot spots, or clusters in random noise because ordinary lumpiness feels too patterned to be chance. Randomness often looks less evenly mixed than intuition expects.

topics.name: Cognitive Bias Taxonomies for Design Practice
topics.description: Academic attempts to organize the large, diffuse space of cognitive biases into taxonomies usable by a specific design discipline (e.g. data visualization), rather than by abstract cognitive theory — the direct precedent for this project's own BiasHeuristic taxonomy.

standalone_findings.description: Proposes a task-based taxonomy of 154 cognitive biases relevant to information visualization design, organized into 7 categories by which analysis/visualization task they affect — explicitly built to be more usable for designers than prior bias taxonomies organized around abstract cognitive theory, while noting limited empirical research documents how most of these biases actually affect real visual data analysis activities.
standalone_findings.source_title: A Task-Based Taxonomy of Cognitive Biases for Information Visualization
standalone_findings.source_venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

topics.name: Confirmation Bias
topics.description: The tendency to seek and interpret evidence in ways that favor existing beliefs or the hypothesis currently in hand — relevant both to the user behavior BECO studies and to the risk of design/UX research itself being conducted to confirm an assumption rather than test it.

biases.name: Confirmation Bias
biases.description: People seek, notice, and interpret evidence in ways that support what they already believe or expect. Once a hypothesis takes hold, contradictory evidence is easy to miss unless the process explicitly looks for it.

biases.name: Congruence Bias
biases.description: When testing a hypothesis, people prefer checks that would confirm it rather than checks that could rule it out. The search strategy itself bends toward saying 'yes' to the current theory.

biases.name: Frequency Illusion
biases.description: After noticing something once, people can feel as if it suddenly appears everywhere. The experience is usually described as a mix of selective noticing and biased interpretation of subsequent encounters rather than a settled standalone experimental law.

biases.name: Semmelweis Reflex
biases.description: A community reflexively rejects evidence because it clashes with established norms, assumptions, or identity. The label invokes the historical Semmelweis story more than a clearly delimited scientific mechanism.

topics.name: Conjunction Fallacy
topics.description: Judging a conjunction of two events (A and B) as more probable than either event alone (A) — the classic 'Linda problem' demonstration that representativeness can override basic probability logic.

biases.name: Conjunction Fallacy
biases.description: People can judge a detailed combined story as more probable than one of its simpler component events, because the richer story feels more representative. The classic example is rating 'Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement' as more likely than 'Linda is a bank teller.'

standalone_findings.description: A series of studies found that the classic Linda conjunction problem's use of the ambiguous term 'probability' leads people to infer nonmathematical meanings of the word; when the wording instead uses 'frequency' (narrowing interpretation to mathematical meanings), conjunction-rule violations drop substantially. Argues that much of the apparent 'fallacy' reflects rational semantic/pragmatic inference about ambiguous everyday language, not a genuine failure of logical reasoning -- a normative reinterpretation, not a dispute of the underlying behavioral pattern (people do rate the conjunction as more probable under 'probability' wording).
standalone_findings.source_title: The 'conjunction fallacy' revisited: how intelligent inferences look like reasoning errors

standalone_findings.description: Across 2 studies (the second an independent replication with a different sample), people who more strongly endorsed conspiracy theories also made more conjunction-rule violations than weaker conspiracists, regardless of contextual framing (neutral, paranormal, or conspiracy) -- a domain-general individual-differences link between conspiracist ideation and conjunction-fallacy susceptibility, discussed in relation to the representativeness heuristic and inferring causal connections between unrelated events.
standalone_findings.source_title: Belief in Conspiracy Theories and Susceptibility to the Conjunction Fallacy

topics.name: Cross-Cultural Replication of Framing & Anchoring Effects
topics.description: Whether classic framing and anchoring effects, originally demonstrated in single Western samples, actually replicate outside them — Many Labs 2's 36-country direct replication of the gain/loss framing paradigm found the effect held in the same direction, though at reduced magnitude.

biases.name: Cross-Cultural Robustness of Framing & Anchoring Effects
biases.description: At least some classic judgment effects designers borrow from behavioral economics do not appear to be limited to Western student samples. The safest reading here is meta-scientific: framing clearly held directionally across many countries, while the anchoring side is genuinely more mixed -- present, but not a clean universal replication.

topics.name: Curiosity Gap (Information Gap Theory)
topics.description: Curiosity as a form of cognitively induced deprivation arising from a perceived gap between what someone knows and wants to know — the direct explanation for why deliberately withholding information drives engagement with headlines, previews, and progress indicators.

biases.name: Curiosity Gap
biases.description: A perceived gap between what someone knows and what they want to know creates an aversive state of deprivation that motivates information-seeking to close it.

standalone_findings.description: A corpus-linguistic analysis of clickbait headlines found writers create Loewenstein's 'information gap' via specific, statistically overrepresented parts-of-speech: definite referring expressions and superlatives/intensifiers. These constructions encourage readers to build new mental 'conceptual files' from the headline's terms while providing little actual content for them, driving readers to click in expectation of filling the gap. Directly explains the linguistic mechanics behind curiosity-gap-driven headline and notification copy in real design practice.
standalone_findings.source_title: You won't believe what's in this paper! Clickbait, relevance and the curiosity gap

topics.name: Decision Fatigue
topics.description: Whether a long sequence of consecutive decisions degrades judgment quality — the famous 'hungry judge' parole study is genuinely disputed at the mechanism level, with a real simulation-based alternative explanation requiring no fatigue at all.

biases.name: Decision Fatigue
biases.description: The quality of decisions degrades after a long sequence of decisions, as if decision-making capacity were a depletable resource -- distinct from Ego Depletion's broader willpower-resource claim, this is specifically about decision-making quality declining with decision volume.

topics.name: Distinction Bias / Joint vs. Separate Evaluation
topics.description: Options evaluated jointly/side-by-side appear more different, and differences are weighted more heavily, than when the same options are evaluated separately.

biases.name: Distinction Bias
biases.description: Small differences between options feel larger when the options are compared side by side than when each is experienced on its own. Comparison mode can manufacture importance that disappears in real use.

topics.name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
topics.description: The classic claim that low-competence people overestimate their own ability more than high-competence people do — and a credible statistical-artifact critique arguing the effect's magnitude has been substantially overstated.

biases.name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
biases.description: Low skill can come with poor self-monitoring, leading some people to rate their own competence too highly. In design work the label is safest when used for self-assessment errors, not as a casual insult for disagreement.

topics.name: Experience Evaluation & Remembered Utility
topics.description: How people retrospectively judge the value of an experience — disproportionately shaped by its peak moment and its ending, not its total duration or average intensity.

biases.name: Duration Neglect
biases.description: When people remember an experience later, its total length often matters less than a few standout moments. Memory of the episode is weighted weakly by duration and more strongly by how it felt at its peak and ending.

biases.name: Fading Affect Bias
biases.description: The emotional sting of negative autobiographical memories tends to fade faster over time than the positive feeling attached to good memories. As time passes, the remembered emotional balance of the past can drift upward.

biases.name: Peak-End Rule
biases.description: People judge an experience mostly by how it felt at its most intense moment and at its end, not by its average or total.

biases.name: Rosy Retrospection
biases.description: People often remember past experiences as better than they felt in the moment. Memory polishes the past, so the remembered version can become more positive than the live experience actually was.

topics.name: Focusing Illusion
topics.description: Overweighting one salient dimension of a decision or future scenario, leading to a distorted forecast of how much that dimension will actually matter to overall satisfaction.

biases.name: Focusing Effect
biases.description: When judging a complex outcome, people overweight the salient feature currently in view and neglect the rest of what will matter in real life. What is easy to think about temporarily feels more important than it really is.

topics.name: Gambler's Fallacy
topics.description: The mistaken belief that past independent random outcomes influence future ones (e.g. a coin is 'due' for tails after a run of heads).

biases.name: Gambler's Fallacy
biases.description: After a run of one outcome, people feel the opposite outcome is 'due' even when each event is objectively independent. The mind mistakes short streaks for evidence that chance should self-correct immediately.

standalone_findings.description: Across three independent laboratory experiments (n=40, 39, 40) using a sequential red/black roulette-color-prediction task, Studer, Limbrick-Oldfield & Clark independently replicated the gambler's fallacy on choice behavior after color runs, and (in Experiment 2) on betting behavior after color runs -- confirming the core streak-driven reversal-prediction effect in a directly comparable binary-prediction paradigm to Barron & Leider (2009). A secondary finding not present in the original study: feedback (winning/losing) streaks did not reliably influence trial-by-trial confidence ratings in either payoff condition, though losing streaks did increase betting amount (interpreted as loss-chasing) -- the confidence dissociation is a genuine extension, not a contradiction of the core replicated effect.
standalone_findings.source_title: ‘Put Your Money Where Your Mouth Is!’: Effects of Streaks on Confidence and Betting in a Binary Choice Task

standalone_findings.description: The same law-of-small-numbers intuition led people to expect each short segment of a random sequence to mirror the overall proportion, making ordinary streaks and local clumps seem overly diagnostic and feeding gambler's-fallacy-style misperception of randomness.
standalone_findings.source_title: Belief in the law of small numbers.

topics.name: Hedonic Adaptation & Affective Forecasting (Impact Bias)
topics.description: People are systematically bad at predicting how happy or unhappy future events will make them (affective forecasting/impact bias), and tend to adapt back to an emotional baseline faster than expected — relevant to how products set expectations about outcomes.

biases.name: Focusing Effect
biases.description: When judging a complex outcome, people overweight the salient feature currently in view and neglect the rest of what will matter in real life. What is easy to think about temporarily feels more important than it really is.

biases.name: Hedonic Adaptation / Impact Bias
biases.description: People adapt faster than expected to positive and negative experiences, and they also mispredict how intense or lasting those feelings will be. New features, rewards, or setbacks rarely feel as transformative for as long as teams or users expect.

standalone_findings.description: Kim & Oswald identify a previously unrecognized methodological weakness (lottery-ticket bias -- unobservable variation in how much people spend on lottery tickets) that had masked lottery windfalls' true effect on happiness in prior research including Brickman et al.'s 1978 study. Correcting for this bias in a large Singapore sample (n=5,626), they find lottery windfalls DO predict substantial improvements in happiness and well-being -- directly disputing the original small-sample finding that lottery winners were no happier than controls.
standalone_findings.source_title: Happy Lottery Winners and Lottery-Ticket Bias

topics.name: Heuristics & Biases
topics.description: The foundational cognitive-shortcut research program (representativeness, availability, anchoring) explaining systematic, predictable errors in human judgment under uncertainty.

biases.name: Anchoring Bias
biases.description: Initial exposure to a number or value ('anchor') skews subsequent judgments and valuations toward that anchor, even when the anchor is arbitrary or irrelevant.

biases.name: Base Rate Fallacy
biases.description: People often underweight general statistical base-rate information when a vivid or representative case description is available, letting the specific story dominate the probabilities.

biases.name: Belief Bias
biases.description: People can judge an argument as logically stronger when its conclusion sounds believable, and weaker when its conclusion sounds implausible, even if the formal logic says otherwise. Plausibility leaks into validity judgment.

biases.name: Clustering Illusion
biases.description: People see meaningful streaks, hot spots, or clusters in random noise because ordinary lumpiness feels too patterned to be chance. Randomness often looks less evenly mixed than intuition expects.

biases.name: Gambler's Fallacy
biases.description: After a run of one outcome, people feel the opposite outcome is 'due' even when each event is objectively independent. The mind mistakes short streaks for evidence that chance should self-correct immediately.

biases.name: Illusion of Validity
biases.description: A judgment can feel highly convincing because the evidence forms a coherent story, even when its real predictive accuracy is weak. Confidence outruns validity when consistency gets mistaken for proof.

biases.name: Information Bias
biases.description: People may seek more information even when that information cannot improve the decision or change the action they should take. Knowing more feels useful or reassuring even when it is instrumentally irrelevant.

biases.name: Insensitivity to Sample Size
biases.description: People often treat results from small samples as if they were much more stable and representative than they really are. Low-N evidence feels cleaner and more reliable than sampling variability allows.

biases.name: Law of Triviality
biases.description: Groups can spend disproportionate time debating small, easy-to-grasp details while under-discussing the harder, more consequential architecture behind them. In software and product work, this is usually called bikeshedding.

biases.name: Less-Is-Better Effect
biases.description: An option can look better when judged on its own than it does when compared side by side with an objectively superior alternative. Separate evaluation can reverse what feels better because people lean on different cues when direct comparison is absent.

biases.name: Occam’s Razor
biases.description: When two explanations or designs solve the same problem equally well, prefer the simpler one with fewer assumptions. In UX discourse, it is often invoked as shorthand for removing needless complexity.

biases.name: Pareto Principle
biases.description: A common rule of thumb that a minority of causes often drives a majority of outcomes, popularly phrased as 80/20. In UX practice it is used to justify prioritizing the few features, issues, or user paths thought to matter most.

standalone_findings.description: People judge the frequency or probability of an event by the ease with which instances or scenarios of it come to mind (availability), rather than by actual frequency — demonstrated experimentally (e.g. participants judging that more English words begin with the letter K than have K as the third letter, when the reverse is true, because words are more easily retrieved by first letter). Availability is driven by factors unrelated to true frequency, such as recency, salience, and imaginability, producing systematic and predictable judgment errors.
standalone_findings.source_title: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability

standalone_findings.description: People underweight merely-probable outcomes relative to certain ones (certainty effect) and discard components shared across choice options (isolation effect); the value function is concave for gains, convex for losses, and steeper for losses than gains (loss aversion); decision weights replace raw probabilities.
standalone_findings.source_title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk

standalone_findings.description: Proposes a task-based taxonomy of 154 cognitive biases relevant to information visualization design, organized into 7 categories by which analysis/visualization task they affect — explicitly built to be more usable for designers than prior bias taxonomies organized around abstract cognitive theory, while noting limited empirical research documents how most of these biases actually affect real visual data analysis activities.
standalone_findings.source_title: A Task-Based Taxonomy of Cognitive Biases for Information Visualization
standalone_findings.source_venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

topics.name: Hindsight Bias
topics.description: The 'I-knew-it-all-along' effect: once an outcome is known, people overestimate how predictable it was beforehand, distorting judgment of past decisions and forecasts.

biases.name: Hindsight Bias
biases.description: After learning an outcome, people overestimate how predictable it was and misremember what they believed beforehand. The past starts to feel more obvious than it actually was at the time.

biases.name: Outcome Bias
biases.description: After the result is known, people judge a past decision by how it turned out instead of by whether it was a good decision given the information available at the time. A lucky bad process can look wise, and a sound process with a bad result can look foolish.

standalone_findings.description: A comprehensive review synthesizes hindsight bias as three related sub-phenomena (memory distortion, beliefs about an event's objective likelihood, and beliefs about one's own predictive ability), driven by cognitive (selective recall, sensemaking), metacognitive (misattributed ease-of-understanding), and motivational (need to see the world as orderly, blame avoidance) mechanisms. Identifies real-world consequences -- myopic attention to a single causal explanation of the past, general overconfidence -- and a genuine debiasing intervention: prompting people to consider alternative causal explanations for an outcome reduces the bias.
standalone_findings.source_title: Hindsight Bias

standalone_findings.description: A meta-analysis of many independent empirical hindsight-bias studies found the effect occurs reliably under some conditions but not universally -- moderated by task familiarity and the type of outcome information presented, with general-knowledge ('almanac') questions producing an unusually large effect -- and that the overall pooled effect magnitude is modest rather than large. An asymmetry in the observed pattern favors a cognitive rather than a purely motivational explanation for the bias.
standalone_findings.source_title: The hindsight bias: A meta-analysis
standalone_findings.source_venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

topics.name: Hot-Hand Belief / Hot-Hand Fallacy
topics.description: The belief that a person on a run of successes ('a hot hand') is more likely to succeed again — genuinely contested in the literature, with some domains showing real streak-dependent performance and others not.

biases.name: Hot-Hand Fallacy
biases.description: People may believe someone on a success streak is more likely to keep succeeding. The catch is that this belief is not simply 'wrong' in every domain: some streak perceptions are illusory, but some hot-hand performance is real.

topics.name: Illusion of Control
topics.description: The tendency to overestimate one's own ability to influence outcomes that are actually determined by chance, especially when situational cues resemble skill-based tasks — relevant to gamified UI that implies control over random outcomes.

biases.name: Illusion of Control
biases.description: People overestimate their ability to control or influence outcomes that are actually determined by chance, especially when skill-relevant cues (choice, competition, familiarity, active involvement, practice) are present even though they have no real bearing on the outcome.

topics.name: Illusory Correlation
topics.description: Perceiving a statistical association between two variables (often a social group and a behavior) that doesn't actually exist, or is much weaker than perceived — a cognitive basis for stereotyping.

biases.name: Illusory Correlation
biases.description: People perceive a meaningful relationship between two traits, groups, or events because the pairing feels salient or memorable, not because a real correlation exists. Distinctive co-occurrences can look diagnostic even when they are just noise.

topics.name: Illusory Truth Effect
topics.description: Whether repeated statements feel more true, independent of whether they actually are — relevant to repeated-claim marketing tactics and misinformation-adjacent design ethics, explained by a 'processing fluency' account: familiarity from repetition gets misread as a signal of truth.

biases.name: Illusory Truth Effect
biases.description: Repeated statements feel truer than new ones, even when repetition adds no new evidence. Familiarity can be misread as credibility.

topics.name: Information Bias
topics.description: Seeking additional information even when that information cannot actually change the decision or action being taken.

biases.name: Information Bias
biases.description: People may seek more information even when that information cannot improve the decision or change the action they should take. Knowing more feels useful or reassuring even when it is instrumentally irrelevant.

topics.name: Insensitivity to Sample Size / Law of Small Numbers
topics.description: Judging small and large samples as equally informative/representative of a population, ignoring how sample size affects statistical reliability.

biases.name: Insensitivity to Sample Size
biases.description: People often treat results from small samples as if they were much more stable and representative than they really are. Low-N evidence feels cleaner and more reliable than sampling variability allows.

topics.name: Moral Luck
topics.description: Moral judgment of an action is influenced by its actual outcome, even when that outcome was outside the actor's control.

biases.name: Moral Luck
biases.description: Once outcomes are known, people often morally re-grade the same action by what happened afterward, even when that outcome was partly outside the actor's control. Bad luck can make identical judgment look more blameworthy than good luck.

standalone_findings.description: Across ten preregistered experiments (N=2043), Kneer & Skoczeń independently confirm that harmful outcomes -- contrasted with neutral outcomes -- increase perceived probability of harm ex post and, consequently, attributions of negligence and culpability, directly supporting Lench et al.'s core moral-luck claim that harm occurring (not just intent) drives harsher blame. The paper explicitly uses 'moral luck' terminology, though frames the primary mechanism as hindsight bias rather than testing individual differences in moral-luck belief as Lench's original design did, and additionally tests and identifies partially effective debiasing strategies.
standalone_findings.source_title: Outcome effects, moral luck and the hindsight bias

topics.name: Negativity Bias
topics.description: The consistent finding that negative information and events exert a stronger psychological effect than equivalent positive ones — one of the most robustly replicated asymmetries in psychology, directly relevant to how error states, warnings, and negative reviews are weighted against positive ones in design.

biases.name: Negativity Bias
biases.description: Negative information, outcomes, and experiences weigh more heavily than equally positive ones. One bad moment can dominate how users remember and judge an otherwise good experience.

standalone_findings.description: Extends the negativity bias (adults attend to, learn from, and use negative information more than positive information) into early child development, arguing the bias is present from infancy -- evident especially in infant social-referencing research -- and exploring its evolutionary and developmental functions. Genuinely extends the phenomenon's known population scope beyond the adult-focused evidence this corpus previously held.
standalone_findings.source_title: Not all emotions are created equal: The negativity bias in social-emotional development

topics.name: Normalcy Bias & Disaster-Preparedness Underestimation
topics.description: Underestimating the probability or extent of a coming disruption because a similar one hasn't happened before — a construct with real theoretical grounding in disaster-response psychology, though without a controlled experimental demonstration of its occurrence or magnitude.

biases.name: Normalcy Bias
biases.description: People can discount warning signs and assume an abnormal situation will stay manageable because 'things are probably still normal.' In practice the label is used most often for delayed action around disasters, crises, or emergencies.

topics.name: Omission Bias
topics.description: A preference for inaction/omission over an equivalent or better action, driven by judging harm caused by inaction as less blameworthy than equivalent harm caused by action.

biases.name: Omission Bias
biases.description: People can judge harm caused by doing something as worse than comparable or greater harm caused by not acting, even when the outcomes favor action. In practice, inaction can feel safer or less blameworthy than an active choice.

topics.name: Ostrich Effect / Selective Avoidance of Bad News
topics.description: Avoiding checking or attending to information that is likely to be negative (e.g. financial losses, health results), even when checking would help decision-making.

biases.name: Ostrich Effect
biases.description: People sometimes avoid looking at information when they expect it to be unpleasant, threatening, or discouraging. Bad news is easier to postpone by not opening the dashboard, statement, or result at all.

topics.name: Outcome Bias
topics.description: Judging the quality of a past decision by how its outcome turned out, rather than by the quality of the decision process available at the time it was made.

biases.name: Moral Luck
biases.description: Once outcomes are known, people often morally re-grade the same action by what happened afterward, even when that outcome was partly outside the actor's control. Bad luck can make identical judgment look more blameworthy than good luck.

biases.name: Outcome Bias
biases.description: After the result is known, people judge a past decision by how it turned out instead of by whether it was a good decision given the information available at the time. A lucky bad process can look wise, and a sound process with a bad result can look foolish.

topics.name: Overconfidence Effect & Optimism Bias
topics.description: The systematic tendency to overestimate one's own abilities or judgment accuracy (overconfidence) and to underestimate one's own risk relative to others (comparative optimism) — including the theoretical work distinguishing overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision as separable components.

biases.name: Hard-Easy Effect
biases.description: Confidence can move in the wrong direction with task difficulty: on hard tasks people often overestimate how well they will do, while on easy tasks they can underestimate it. Difficulty distorts calibration, not just confidence level.

biases.name: Illusion of Validity
biases.description: A judgment can feel highly convincing because the evidence forms a coherent story, even when its real predictive accuracy is weak. Confidence outruns validity when consistency gets mistaken for proof.

biases.name: Overconfidence / Optimism Bias
biases.description: People systematically overrate what they know, how well they will do, or how likely good outcomes are for them. In product work this shows up as underweighted risk, rosy self-assessments, and overconfident plans.

biases.name: Pessimism Bias
biases.description: People can overestimate how likely bad outcomes are for themselves or for a plan, treating negative futures as more probable than they really are. In practice this shows up as forecasts that lean too hard toward failure, loss, or disappointment.

topics.name: Planning Fallacy
topics.description: Whether people reliably underestimate how long tasks will take — real in engineering/management contexts specifically, but the popularized universal framing oversimplifies a more mixed evidence base, and even the 'small tasks overestimated, large underestimated' claim may partly be a statistical artifact.

biases.name: Planning Fallacy
biases.description: People often predict that tasks or projects will finish sooner than they actually do, especially when they focus on the ideal plan instead of comparable past outcomes. The broad 'people always underestimate time' version is more overstated than the evidence supports.

biases.name: Time-Saving Bias
biases.description: People misjudge how much time a speed increase will actually save. We intuitively undervalue moving from slow to moderately faster speeds and overvalue squeezing a little extra speed out of an already fast process.

topics.name: Present Bias & Hyperbolic Discounting
topics.description: Disproportionate weighting of immediate rewards/costs over future ones, and the discounting models (hyperbolic, quasi-hyperbolic) used to formalize it.

biases.name: Present Bias
biases.description: People place disproportionately high weight on immediate rewards/costs relative to future ones, leading to procrastination and undersaving.

biases.name: Restraint Bias
biases.description: People overestimate how well their future self will resist temptation or stay in control around triggers. Feeling strong now leads them to take exposure risks that make later self-control failures more likely.

standalone_findings.description: Across a field study (MIT executive-education students given the choice to self-impose grade-consequential deadlines for three papers) and follow-up lab studies, people voluntarily self-impose costly, binding deadlines to counteract their own anticipated procrastination, and doing so measurably improves task-completion timing and performance relative to no deadline at all -- but self-set deadlines are not optimally chosen for maximum performance and are less effective than deadlines of equivalent stringency imposed externally (evenly spaced deadlines set by the instructor outperformed self-chosen ones).
standalone_findings.source_title: Procrastination, Deadlines, and Performance: Self-Control by Precommitment

topics.name: Price/Marketing Placebo Effects & Expectation-Driven Experience
topics.description: Whether price and marketing cues change genuine subjective — and sometimes measurable neural — experience of a product or service, independent of any real difference in the product itself. Directly relevant to premium pricing and polished visual design shaping perceived quality before any actual use.

biases.name: Expectation Bias
biases.description: What people expect beforehand can alter what they later feel, notice, or report about the same experience. Prior cues such as price, branding, warnings, or promises can bias downstream judgments so the product seems better or worse before anything objective has changed.

biases.name: Price Placebo Effect
biases.description: Price and other marketing cues can change the experience itself, not just what people say about it afterward. A 'premium' frame can make the same product feel more effective, pleasant, or valuable.

topics.name: Probability Neglect / Affective Probability Insensitivity
topics.description: Emotionally vivid outcomes get weighted based on how they feel rather than their actual probability, especially for very low- or very high-probability events.

biases.name: Neglect of Probability
biases.description: When an outcome is vivid or emotionally charged, people can react to the possibility itself while underweighting how likely it actually is. A 1% chance and a 99% chance can evoke surprisingly similar concern if the imagined outcome is intense enough.

topics.name: Risk Compensation / Peltzman Effect
topics.description: People take on more risk once a safety measure is introduced, partially offsetting the safety benefit the measure was meant to provide.

biases.name: Peltzman Effect
biases.description: When a product, policy, or environment feels safer, people may respond by taking more risk elsewhere, offsetting some of the intended safety gain. The extra protection gets spent behaviorally instead of being preserved fully.

topics.name: Subadditivity Effect / Support Theory
topics.description: The judged probability of a whole event is smaller than the sum of the judged probabilities of its explicitly-unpacked component parts — a violation of standard probability theory.

biases.name: Subadditivity Effect
biases.description: When an event is unpacked into specific parts, the summed judged probabilities of those parts can exceed the judged probability of the broader whole. Detailed breakdowns can therefore feel more likely than the same outcome described in a packed, generic way.

topics.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
topics.description: Continuing to invest in a failing course of action because of prior, non-recoverable investment — heavily invoked in retention design ('don't lose your progress'), and the subject of a recent measurement-validity critique of the field's own standard vignettes.

biases.name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
biases.description: People continue investing in a losing course of action because of what they've already invested, even when that prior investment is irrecoverable and irrelevant to the rational forward-looking decision.

topics.name: Survivorship Bias
topics.description: The popular 'survivorship bias' retelling (reinforce where the returning planes have no bullet holes) flattens a genuinely rigorous piece of applied statistics — Wald's real method explicitly modeled the unobserved damage distribution across planes that never returned, not just a rule of thumb about visible survivors.

biases.name: Survivorship Bias
biases.description: When you only look at the cases that made it through the funnel, you can draw the wrong lesson about what causes success or failure. Visible winners are not a representative sample.

topics.name: Zero-Risk Bias
topics.description: A preference for completely eliminating one risk entirely over achieving a larger reduction in a different, larger risk — prioritizing the feeling of total certainty over expected-value-optimal risk reduction.

biases.name: Zero-Risk Bias
biases.description: When comparing risk-reduction options, people often prefer completely eliminating one risk over achieving a larger total reduction distributed across risks. The pull of a clean 'zero' can outweigh the numerically better trade-off.

domains.name: Social & Self Attribution
domains.description: How people explain their own and others' behavior, and the systematic errors in that explanation.

topics.name: Actor-Observer Bias
topics.description: The tendency to attribute one's own behavior to situational factors while attributing others' identical behavior to their disposition/character — related to but distinct from the fundamental attribution error.

biases.name: Actor-Observer Bias
biases.description: The popular claim says people explain their own behavior with situational causes but explain other people's behavior with dispositional causes. The broad textbook version is more sweeping than the best evidence supports.

biases.name: Trait Ascription Bias
biases.description: People tend to see their own behavior as flexible and situation-dependent while seeing other people's behavior as more fixed, trait-like, and predictable. We grant ourselves nuance more readily than we grant others.

topics.name: Age-Related Positivity Effect
topics.description: Older adults, relative to younger adults, preferentially attend to and remember positive information over negative information — an emotion-regulation-linked shift distinct from general 'positivity bias.'

biases.name: Positivity Effect
biases.description: Older adults often attend to and remember positive information relatively more than negative information, compared with younger adults. This is a specific aging-and-emotion-regulation finding, not a generic optimism claim.

topics.name: Barnum / Forer Effect
topics.description: People rate vague, generic personality descriptions as highly accurate and personally tailored to them — the mechanism behind horoscopes, generic 'personalized' copy, and similar practices.

biases.name: Barnum Effect
biases.description: People accept vague, high-base-rate descriptions as uniquely accurate when those descriptions are framed as personalized feedback. Generic statements can feel uncannily specific if the context promises individual insight.

topics.name: Belief in a Just World / Just-World Hypothesis
topics.description: The belief that the world is fundamentally fair, so people generally get what they deserve — a belief that can lead to victim-blaming and rationalizing observed misfortune.

biases.name: Defensive Attribution Hypothesis
biases.description: When judging an accident or misfortune, people can assign less blame to actors they identify with and more blame to targets who feel unlike them. The attribution protects the observer's own sense that they would be safe or justified in a similar situation.

biases.name: Just-World Hypothesis
biases.description: People are motivated to believe the world is fundamentally fair, which can make them infer that outcomes were deserved. This often shows up as victim blaming or overconfidence that institutions reward merit cleanly.

topics.name: Better-Than-Average Effect / Illusory Superiority
topics.description: Most people rate themselves as above average on desirable traits and abilities, which is statistically impossible for the whole population.

biases.name: Illusory Superiority
biases.description: People often rate their own abilities, traits, or judgment as better than average, even when that cannot be true for most of a group at once. Self-evaluation drifts upward when comparison targets are vague or flattering.

topics.name: Bias Blind Spot
topics.description: People recognize cognitive biases far more readily in others' judgments than in their own.

biases.name: Bias Blind Spot
biases.description: People readily spot bias in other people while seeing their own judgments as comparatively objective. The mind gives itself a special exemption from the very distortions it recognizes elsewhere.

topics.name: Cheerleader Effect / Group Attractiveness Effect
topics.description: Individual faces are judged as more attractive when seen as part of a group than when seen alone.

biases.name: Cheerleader Effect
biases.description: A person can look more attractive when seen as part of a group than when seen alone. Group context shifts perception of the individual, not just the group.

topics.name: Choice-Supportive Bias / Misremembering
topics.description: After making a choice, people tend to misremember the rejected and chosen options as more different — and more favorable to the choice made — than they actually were.

biases.name: Choice-Supportive Bias
biases.description: People remember a past choice as better than it really was, attributing more positives to what they chose and more negatives to what they rejected. Memory becomes a quiet advocate for the committed option.

topics.name: Cognitive Dissonance
topics.description: Whether people resolve the discomfort of acting against their private beliefs by changing the belief itself — the classic $1-vs-$20 demonstration was only marginally significant in its own data, and a 39-lab, N=4,898 replication found the specific choice mechanism didn't hold up at scale.

biases.name: Effort Justification
biases.description: After paying a meaningful effort cost to get something, people can value it more highly than the thing itself objectively warrants. Effort gets retrospectively rationalized into value.

biases.name: Post-purchase Rationalization
biases.description: After choosing or buying, people tend to defend the decision by upgrading the chosen option and downgrading the rejected alternatives. The mind edits evaluations to make the commitment feel better justified.

standalone_findings.description: 71 male students performed a deliberately boring task, then were paid $1 or $20 to tell the next participant the task had been enjoyable. Participants paid only $1 subsequently rated the task as significantly more enjoyable than a no-payment control group — the opposite of what a simple reward-reinforcement account would predict — while the $20 group showed no such shift. Explained as cognitive dissonance reduction: with only $1 as external justification for lying, participants had to internally rationalize their statement by actually changing their attitude; with $20, ample external justification meant no such pressure existed. The results were only marginally statistically significant (p≈.08-.15, two-tailed) — a nuance rarely mentioned in how the study is popularly cited.
standalone_findings.effect_size: One Dollar condition mean enjoyment rating ≈ +1.20 vs. Control ≈ -0.62 (rating scale, significant at .08 level); One Dollar vs. Twenty Dollar difference significant at .15 level
standalone_findings.source_title: Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance
standalone_findings.source_venue: The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology

standalone_findings.description: A pre-registered multi-lab replication across 39 labs in 19 countries (N=4,898) tested the core induced-compliance mechanism directly: writing a counterattitudinal essay under high choice vs. low choice. The primary analysis found no significant difference between the high-choice and low-choice conditions — the specific mechanism Festinger & Carlsmith's original $1/$20 manipulation was designed to demonstrate did not replicate at scale. A real attitude difference was found between writing a counterattitudinal essay at all versus a neutral essay, so something real is happening — but the results call into question whether the classic 'induced-compliance paradigm' actually demonstrates cognitive dissonance the way it has long been assumed to.
standalone_findings.source_title: A Multilab Replication of the Induced-Compliance Paradigm of Cognitive Dissonance
standalone_findings.source_venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

topics.name: Construal Level Theory & Psychological Distance
topics.description: Trope & Liberman's theory that psychologically distant things — future, hypothetical, physically far, socially distant — are represented more abstractly than psychologically near things, and this shapes evaluation and decision-making.

standalone_findings.description: Psychological distance (temporal, spatial, social, and hypothetical) is a unified, egocentric construct: the farther an object or event is from the self in the here-and-now, the more abstractly (higher construal level) it is mentally represented, and the four distance dimensions are cognitively related to one another and similarly influence -- and are influenced by -- construal level, prediction, preference, and action.
standalone_findings.source_title: Construal-level theory of psychological distance

topics.name: Cross-Race Effect / Own-Race Bias
topics.description: People are more accurate at recognizing and distinguishing faces from their own race than faces from other races.

biases.name: Cross-Race Effect
biases.description: People are usually better at recognizing and telling apart faces from their own racial group than faces from another group. The effect is not just a verbal belief that “they all look alike” — it shows up in actual memory and discrimination performance.

topics.name: Curse of Knowledge
topics.description: Once someone knows something, they find it hard to model what it's like not to know it — leading experts/designers to underestimate how confusing their own interfaces or explanations are to novices.

biases.name: Curse of Knowledge
biases.description: Once people know something, it becomes hard for them to reconstruct what it is like not to know it. Experts systematically overestimate what novices can infer, notice, or understand unaided.

biases.name: Projection Bias
biases.description: People often assume other people share their own current preferences, reactions, or priorities more than they really do. In product work, this is the classic trap of designing for yourself and treating your current mental state as representative.

standalone_findings.description: An experiment found that when people are primed to see a pattern as visually salient in a data visualization, they predict naive viewers will find the same pattern salient too -- despite explicit instructions to set their own knowledge aside. Demonstrates the curse of knowledge extends beyond verbal/conceptual judgment into visual perception itself, directly explaining why data communicators can fail to connect with audiences who don't share their prior context.
standalone_findings.source_title: The Curse of Knowledge in Visual Data Communication
standalone_findings.source_venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
