standalone_findings.description: Seven large-sample experiments re-estimating the effect size of curse-of-knowledge-driven egocentric errors in false-belief reasoning (adults incorrectly attributing their own privileged knowledge to a less-informed target when the egocentric response is plausible) found the true effect is real but less than half the magnitude of an earlier report -- the earlier study was underpowered (less than 33% power to detect an effect this size). An honest downward revision, not a null result: the effect replicates in direction, but its practical real-world impact on perspective-taking may be smaller than previously assumed.
standalone_findings.effect_size: True effect estimated at less than half the magnitude of the original reported effect
standalone_findings.source_title: Do Adults Show a Curse of Knowledge in False-Belief Reasoning? A Robust Estimate of the True Effect Size

topics.name: Declinism / Perceived Decline
topics.description: A belief that a society, institution, or domain is in decline relative to an idealized past, often more due to psychological bias than actual historical trend.

biases.name: Declinism
biases.description: People can read the present as evidence of decline because the past gets remembered more selectively or nostalgically than it really was. “Things are getting worse” can feel like a plain observation when it is partly driven by memory and exposure bias.

topics.name: Defensive Attribution Hypothesis
topics.description: People assign less blame to an accident's actor the more personally they identify with that actor, protecting their own sense of safety from a similar accident.

biases.name: Defensive Attribution Hypothesis
biases.description: When judging an accident or misfortune, people can assign less blame to actors they identify with and more blame to targets who feel unlike them. The attribution protects the observer's own sense that they would be safe or justified in a similar situation.

topics.name: Egocentric Bias
topics.description: Recalling or interpreting the past in a self-favoring way, including overestimating one's own contribution to a joint effort.

biases.name: Egocentric Bias
biases.description: Our own actions, effort, and reasons are more mentally available to us than other people's, so shared events can look more self-centered than they really were. People may overclaim their contribution or interpret the same history from a self-favoring vantage point.

topics.name: Extrinsic Incentives Bias / Motivation Attribution
topics.description: Attributing other people's behavior to extrinsic incentives/rewards while attributing one's own identical behavior to intrinsic motivation — an attributional asymmetry distinct from the overjustification effect's focus on one's own motivation being undermined by rewards.

biases.name: Extrinsic Incentive Error
biases.description: People often assume other people are driven mainly by pay, status, or other external rewards, while viewing their own motives as more intrinsic. The result is a self-other asymmetry in how motivation gets explained.

topics.name: False Consensus Effect
topics.description: Overestimating how much other people share one's own beliefs, preferences, or behaviors.

biases.name: False Consensus Effect
biases.description: People overestimate how many other people share their own beliefs, choices, or habits. Our own view feels more normal and representative than it really is.

biases.name: Projection Bias
biases.description: People often assume other people share their own current preferences, reactions, or priorities more than they really do. In product work, this is the classic trap of designing for yourself and treating your current mental state as representative.

topics.name: Fundamental Attribution Error
topics.description: The tendency to over-attribute other people's behavior to their disposition or personality and under-attribute it to situational factors, even when the situational constraint is made explicit.

biases.name: Actor-Observer Bias
biases.description: The popular claim says people explain their own behavior with situational causes but explain other people's behavior with dispositional causes. The broad textbook version is more sweeping than the best evidence supports.

biases.name: Group Attribution Error
biases.description: People overgeneralize between individuals and groups: one member's traits get projected onto the whole group, and a group's actions get projected back onto each member. The shortcut feels efficient but can flatten real within-group differences.

biases.name: Ultimate Attribution Error
biases.description: In intergroup settings, people often give their own group more charitable causal stories than the out-group: bad acts by “them” look dispositional, while good acts by “them” get explained away as luck or exception. It is a specifically intergroup version of attribution bias, with prejudice embedded in the explanation pattern.

standalone_findings.description: Lay attributional reasoning shows a consistent, systematic bias toward dispositional (trait-based) explanations of others' behavior and away from situational explanations, even when situational causes are salient and sufficient -- termed by Ross the 'fundamental attribution error.'
standalone_findings.source_title: The Intuitive Psychologist And His Shortcomings: Distortions in the Attribution Process

standalone_findings.description: Observers who read a pro- or anti-Castro essay inferred the writer's true attitude matched the essay's position even when explicitly told the writer had been assigned that position and had no choice -- demonstrating that a clear, sufficient situational explanation for behavior does not eliminate the tendency to draw dispositional inferences from it.
standalone_findings.source_title: The attribution of attitudes

standalone_findings.description: The correspondence bias (fundamental attribution error) arises from at least four distinct mechanisms -- lack of awareness of situational constraints, unrealistic expectations about how a 'normal' person would behave, inflated categorization of behavior as trait-diagnostic, and incomplete correction from an initial dispositional anchor -- rather than a single unitary cause; some cross-cultural work (e.g. on East Asian samples, cited within the broader literature this review engages) finds the effect attenuated or reversed relative to Western samples, making claims of a fully universal, culture-independent bias disputed rather than settled.
standalone_findings.source_title: The correspondence bias

topics.name: Halo Effect
topics.description: A positive or negative impression on one trait biasing judgment of unrelated traits — the broader, older construct behind why visual polish also biases perceived trustworthiness and competence, distinct from the narrower aesthetics-usability question of whether it improves actual task performance.

biases.name: Halo Effect
biases.description: A positive impression of someone or something in one dimension (e.g. appearance) causes an unwarranted positive inference in unrelated dimensions (e.g. competence, trustworthiness).

topics.name: Illusion of Asymmetric Insight
topics.description: Believing one understands other people, or a group, better than those people or that group understand themselves.

biases.name: Illusion of Asymmetric Insight
biases.description: People tend to believe they understand other people better than those people understand them. We treat our own inner life as richly diagnostic while reading other people from their outward behavior with more confidence than they deserve.

topics.name: Illusion of External Agency
topics.description: Misattributing an outcome that was actually self-generated to the intentional influence of an external agent.

biases.name: Illusion of External Agency
biases.description: People can misattribute a self-generated outcome or feeling of fit to an outside agent's intention, insight, or influence. The strongest backing found here is a narrower version: mistaking one's own generated satisfaction with an outcome for evidence that an external agent caused or wisely arranged it.

topics.name: Illusion of Transparency
topics.description: Overestimating how visible one's own internal emotional or mental states are to outside observers.

biases.name: Illusion of Transparency
biases.description: People overestimate how visible their internal thoughts, feelings, or nervousness are to other people. What feels obvious from the inside often leaks out far less than we think.

standalone_findings.description: Managers overestimate how accurately their negative feedback is perceived by employees during performance appraisals -- a transparency illusion driven by managers' insufficient motivation to communicate with effortful precision, not by employee misperception. The illusion is stronger for negative feedback and is associated with more indirect manager communication; interventions were shown to mitigate it. An internal meta-analysis of 11 additional file-drawer studies confirmed a moderate, publication-bias-free effect size (d=0.43).
standalone_findings.effect_size: d = 0.43 (internal meta-analysis of 11 file-drawer studies, N=1887)
standalone_findings.source_title: The illusion of transparency in performance appraisals: When and why accuracy motivation explains unintentional feedback inflation
standalone_findings.source_venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

topics.name: Implicit Associations / Implicit Cognition
topics.description: Automatic, often unconscious associative links between concepts, commonly measured via reaction-time-based tests such as the Implicit Association Test — a large and genuinely contested research literature.

biases.name: Implicit Associations
biases.description: People can show fast, automatic associative links between concepts and attributes even when those links are not available or acceptable in explicit self-report. In practice the term usually refers to relative association patterns inferred indirectly from tasks such as the Implicit Association Test.

biases.name: Implicit Stereotypes
biases.description: Group cues can automatically activate stereotype-linked traits or expectations before a person consciously endorses, rejects, or corrects them. This is narrower than stereotyping in general: it is specifically about fast, often involuntary category-trait activation.

topics.name: In-Group/Out-Group Bias
topics.description: The tendency to favor members of one's own group over outsiders, robust even under minimal or arbitrary group assignment — relevant to social-proof framing, community features, and identity-based segmentation in product design.

biases.name: Cross-Race Effect
biases.description: People are usually better at recognizing and telling apart faces from their own racial group than faces from another group. The effect is not just a verbal belief that “they all look alike” — it shows up in actual memory and discrimination performance.

biases.name: Group Attribution Error
biases.description: People overgeneralize between individuals and groups: one member's traits get projected onto the whole group, and a group's actions get projected back onto each member. The shortcut feels efficient but can flatten real within-group differences.

biases.name: In-Group Bias
biases.description: Simply sorting people into 'us' and 'them' can skew trust, generosity, cooperation, and whose perspective gets believed. Designers run into it whenever identity cues change how fairly people are treated.

biases.name: Out-Group Homogeneity Bias
biases.description: People tend to see members of an out-group as more alike than members of their own group. 'They are all the same' becomes the default impression more easily than it does for 'us'.

biases.name: Prejudice
biases.description: Prejudice is a pre-judged evaluation of a social group or its members, where category membership drives liking, dislike, suspicion, or threat perception before individual evidence does. In practice it is broader than one single bias effect: it bundles attitudes, feelings, and judgment tendencies toward groups.

biases.name: Ultimate Attribution Error
biases.description: In intergroup settings, people often give their own group more charitable causal stories than the out-group: bad acts by “them” look dispositional, while good acts by “them” get explained away as luck or exception. It is a specifically intergroup version of attribution bias, with prejudice embedded in the explanation pattern.

topics.name: Moral Credential Effect / Licensing via Credentials
topics.description: Having an established track record of ethical behavior or attitudes can make people feel licensed to act less ethically afterward.

biases.name: Moral Credential Effect
biases.description: After establishing themselves as moral, fair, or non-prejudiced, people may feel more permitted to act in a less ethical or less egalitarian way afterward. Prior virtue gets interpreted as a license.

topics.name: Naïve Cynicism
topics.description: Expecting other people to be more biased or self-interested in their judgments than those people actually are — the mirror-image counterpart to naïve realism.

biases.name: Naïve Cynicism
biases.description: People can overestimate how biased, strategic, or self-interested other people's judgments are. Suspicion itself becomes biased, so disagreement gets read as ulterior motive faster than reality warrants.

topics.name: Naïve Realism
topics.description: The conviction that one's own perception of a situation is objective and unbiased, so that others who see it differently must be uninformed, irrational, or biased.

biases.name: Naïve Realism
biases.description: People experience their own view as a straightforward reading of reality and treat disagreement as evidence that other people are uninformed, irrational, or biased. What feels like 'just seeing the facts' is often already an interpretation.

topics.name: Not Invented Here (NIH) Syndrome
topics.description: An organizational/individual bias favoring internally developed solutions over externally sourced ones, even when the external option is objectively as good or better — relevant to build-vs-buy product decisions.

biases.name: Not Invented Here
biases.description: Teams devalue external ideas, tools, or solutions simply because they came from outside the group. 'Ours' feels safer, smarter, or more legitimate than something imported, even when the outside option is better.

biases.name: Semmelweis Reflex
biases.description: A community reflexively rejects evidence because it clashes with established norms, assumptions, or identity. The label invokes the historical Semmelweis story more than a clearly delimited scientific mechanism.

topics.name: Prejudice
topics.description: The general affective/cognitive construct of holding a pre-formed, often negative, attitude toward members of a social group.

biases.name: Prejudice
biases.description: Prejudice is a pre-judged evaluation of a social group or its members, where category membership drives liking, dislike, suspicion, or threat perception before individual evidence does. In practice it is broader than one single bias effect: it bundles attitudes, feelings, and judgment tendencies toward groups.

topics.name: Psychological Essentialism / Social Essentialism
topics.description: Believing that social categories reflect a fixed, immutable, deep underlying 'essence,' rather than being socially constructed groupings.

biases.name: Essentialism
biases.description: Essentialism treats a social category as if it reflects a deep, fixed, natural essence rather than a contingent or socially constructed grouping. Once a category feels natural and immutable, within-group variation gets easier to ignore.

topics.name: Reactive Devaluation
topics.description: A proposal or concession is devalued specifically because it comes from an adversary or opposing party, independent of the proposal's actual merits.

biases.name: Reactive Devaluation
biases.description: A proposal can lose value in your eyes simply because it comes from an adversary or distrusted out-group. The source label poisons evaluation before the content gets a fair read.

topics.name: Selective Perception
topics.description: People selectively interpret ambiguous or mixed evidence (e.g. a contested event) in a way that favors their own pre-existing group identity or expectations.

biases.name: Selective Perception
biases.description: What people think they are seeing is filtered by loyalties, expectations, and prior beliefs. Two people can witness the same event yet experience meaningfully different versions of it.

standalone_findings.description: A literature synthesis and formal model found only limited support exists for the more extreme variants of the selective-perception hypothesis -- much of what is attributed to selective/biased perception may instead be consistent with ordinary Bayesian updating on ambiguous information, once research-design flaws (failing to control for prior preferences/information) are accounted for. A genuine normative and methodological challenge to the strong form of the hypothesis, not a claim that no perceptual/interpretive bias exists at all.
standalone_findings.source_title: Misperceptions About Perceptual Bias

standalone_findings.description: Executives from different company departments, reading the identical business case study, disproportionately identified the problem most relevant to their own department as the case's most important issue -- a classic demonstration that professional role and departmental identification shape selective attention and interpretation of identical information, in a business/organizational paradigm distinct from Hastorf & Cantril's shared-event perception study.
standalone_findings.source_title: Selective Perception: A Note on the Departmental Identifications of Executives

topics.name: Self-Consistency Bias
topics.description: Overestimating how consistent one's past attitudes and behaviors were with one's current ones.

biases.name: Self-Consistency Bias
biases.description: People can reconstruct their memories of past attitudes, feelings, or behavior so they look more consistent with who they believe they are now. The past gets edited toward the present self-story.

topics.name: Self-Serving Bias
topics.description: The tendency to attribute successes to one's own ability and failures to external circumstances, protecting self-esteem.

biases.name: Egocentric Bias
biases.description: Our own actions, effort, and reasons are more mentally available to us than other people's, so shared events can look more self-centered than they really were. People may overclaim their contribution or interpret the same history from a self-favoring vantage point.

biases.name: Self-Serving Bias
biases.description: People tend to credit successes to their own ability or character while blaming failures on situation, luck, or unfair circumstances. The same outcome data gets narrated differently depending on whether it protects the self.

topics.name: Spotlight Effect
topics.description: People overestimate how much others notice and remember their appearance and actions — an egocentric anchoring-and-adjustment bias.

biases.name: Spotlight Effect
biases.description: People overestimate how much other people notice their appearance, mistakes, and behavior. Our own experience is so vivid to us that we assume it is much more visible to everyone else than it really is.

standalone_findings.description: In pay-what-you-want pricing settings, customers perceive greater attention on themselves (vs. others) -- especially in the presence of distant (vs. close) others -- causing them to initially anchor their willingness-to-pay on their own internal reference price, a spotlight-effect-driven anchoring pattern. This anchoring effect is adjusted downward when external reference prices are present. An independent research team applies the spotlight effect to a genuinely new, design/marketing-relevant domain: consumer pricing decisions.
standalone_findings.source_title: Exploring the role of spotlight effect in pay-what-you-want (PWYW) pricing—An anchoring and adjustment perspective

topics.name: Stereotyping
topics.description: The general cognitive process of applying group-level generalizations to individual group members, independent of any specific stereotype's content.

biases.name: Essentialism
biases.description: Essentialism treats a social category as if it reflects a deep, fixed, natural essence rather than a contingent or socially constructed grouping. Once a category feels natural and immutable, within-group variation gets easier to ignore.

biases.name: Implicit Stereotypes
biases.description: Group cues can automatically activate stereotype-linked traits or expectations before a person consciously endorses, rejects, or corrects them. This is narrower than stereotyping in general: it is specifically about fast, often involuntary category-trait activation.

biases.name: Prejudice
biases.description: Prejudice is a pre-judged evaluation of a social group or its members, where category membership drives liking, dislike, suspicion, or threat perception before individual evidence does. In practice it is broader than one single bias effect: it bundles attitudes, feelings, and judgment tendencies toward groups.

biases.name: Stereotyping
biases.description: People use category labels to fill in missing information about others, inferring traits or expectations from group membership rather than individual evidence. This can speed judgment, but it also distorts perception and decision-making.

topics.name: System Justification
topics.description: A motivated tendency to defend and rationalize existing social, economic, or political arrangements as fair and legitimate, even when they disadvantage the person doing the justifying.

biases.name: System Justification
biases.description: People are motivated to see existing institutions, hierarchies, and arrangements as legitimate and fair, even when those arrangements disadvantage them. That motive can make the status quo feel natural, deserved, or harder to challenge than it objectively is.

topics.name: Third-Person Effect
topics.description: People believe that media or persuasive messages influence other people more than they influence themselves.

biases.name: Third-Person Effect
biases.description: People tend to think persuasive or harmful media messages affect other people more than themselves. We imagine ourselves as relatively immune while assuming others are easier to sway.

topics.name: Trait Ascription Bias
topics.description: Viewing one's own personality and behavior as more variable and context-dependent than other people's, whose behavior is seen as reflecting fixed, predictable traits.

biases.name: Trait Ascription Bias
biases.description: People tend to see their own behavior as flexible and situation-dependent while seeing other people's behavior as more fixed, trait-like, and predictable. We grant ourselves nuance more readily than we grant others.

topics.name: Unrealistic Pessimism / Pessimism Bias
topics.description: Systematically overestimating the likelihood of negative future outcomes happening to oneself — the mirror case of optimism bias.

biases.name: Pessimism Bias
biases.description: People can overestimate how likely bad outcomes are for themselves or for a plan, treating negative futures as more probable than they really are. In practice this shows up as forecasts that lean too hard toward failure, loss, or disappointment.

standalone_findings.description: Rose, Endo, Windschitl & Suls independently replicate Kruger & Burrus' bidirectional comparative-forecasting pattern using the direct self-vs-peer comparison method: across US and Japanese samples, participants were unrealistically optimistic about infrequent/negative events but unrealistically pessimistic about frequent/negative events, confirming the same egocentric-processing asymmetry holds cross-culturally when measured directly (though an indirect measurement method produced culturally-divergent results, a genuine methodological boundary condition).
standalone_findings.source_title: Cultural Differences in Unrealistic Optimism and Pessimism: The Role of Egocentrism and Direct Versus Indirect Comparison Measures

topics.name: Zero-Sum Bias / Zero-Sum Thinking
topics.description: Perceiving a situation as zero-sum (one party's gain necessarily costing another) when resources or outcomes are not actually fixed or mutually exclusive.

biases.name: Zero-Sum Bias
biases.description: People can intuitively read a situation as win-lose even when the resource is not actually fixed. One person's gain feels like it must come out of someone else's share, even in genuinely non-zero-sum systems.

domains.name: Social Influence & Persuasion
domains.description: How other people and social context sway behavior or belief.

topics.name: Anthropomorphism
topics.description: Attributing human traits, emotions, or intentions to non-human entities, including software, AI assistants, and products.

biases.name: Anthropomorphism
biases.description: People attribute human traits, feelings, intentions, or motives to non-human things such as products, bots, brands, animals, or algorithms. Human-like cues invite social interpretation.

topics.name: Authority & Credibility Signals in Persuasion
topics.description: Whether perceived authority and credibility cues (uniforms, status signals, expertise indicators) increase compliance and persuasion — one of Cialdini's core Influence principles, now backed in this corpus alongside social proof, reciprocity, and consistency.

biases.name: Authority
biases.description: People are more likely to trust or comply with a message when it is associated with perceived expertise, legitimacy, or high-status authority cues. In design, those cues can come from credentials, uniforms, institutional affiliation, verified badges, or expert endorsement.

standalone_findings.description: In a street field experiment, pedestrians followed a confederate's jaywalking violation of a 'Do Not Walk' signal significantly more often when the confederate was dressed to signal high social status than when dressed to signal low status — a pure status/authority visual cue, with no verbal claim of expertise or legitimacy, measurably increasing bystander compliance with a norm-violating behavior.
standalone_findings.source_title: Status factors in pedestrian violation of traffic signals

topics.name: Bandwagon Effect / Herding Behavior
topics.description: People adopting a behavior, belief, or choice because others are doing so, independent of their own private information — including the formal theoretical models of herd behavior and informational cascades that explain why it can be individually rational yet collectively inefficient.

biases.name: Herding Behavior
biases.description: When people can see what others chose, they may copy the crowd instead of relying on their own information. A few early visible choices can snowball into a self-reinforcing adoption pattern.

topics.name: Bystander Effect / Diffusion of Responsibility
topics.description: The finding that individuals are less likely to help in an emergency when other people are present, due to diffusion of responsibility — attenuates or reverses under genuinely dangerous conditions.

biases.name: Bystander Effect
biases.description: The more people who seem to be present, the less personally responsible any one person may feel to help. Visible others can shift a situation from 'I should act' to 'someone else probably will.'

topics.name: Commitment & Consistency (Foot-in-the-Door)
topics.description: Whether agreeing to a small initial request makes someone more likely to comply with a larger one later — real, but driven by several distinct psychological processes rather than one, which is also why it sometimes fails or backfires.

biases.name: Foot-in-the-Door
biases.description: Securing agreement to a small initial request substantially increases compliance with a larger subsequent request, driven by a desire to act consistently with one's prior self-image.

topics.name: Door-in-the-Face & Low-Ball Compliance Techniques
topics.description: Sequential-request compliance techniques that work in the opposite direction from foot-in-the-door: door-in-the-face (an extreme request refused, then a smaller one) and low-ball (escalating the cost of a commitment after it's made).

biases.name: Door-in-the-Face Technique
biases.description: Opening with a request expected to be refused, then retreating to the smaller request actually wanted, produces more compliance with that smaller request than asking for it directly -- read by the target as a concession worth reciprocating.

biases.name: Low-Ball Technique
biases.description: Securing agreement to a low initial cost or commitment, then revealing a higher true cost afterward, yields more final compliance than disclosing the full cost upfront -- driven by commitment to the earlier decision, not merely momentum from having already said yes.

topics.name: Identifiable / Identified Victim Effect
topics.description: People are more moved to help, and donate more, toward a single identified victim than toward a larger, statistically-described group facing the same need.

biases.name: Identifiable Victim Effect
biases.description: People often feel a stronger urge to help when harm is attached to one concrete, identified person than when the same harm is described statistically or spread across a group. A face, name, or single story can outweigh larger but abstract suffering.

topics.name: In-Group/Out-Group Bias
topics.description: The tendency to favor members of one's own group over outsiders, robust even under minimal or arbitrary group assignment — relevant to social-proof framing, community features, and identity-based segmentation in product design.

biases.name: Cross-Race Effect
biases.description: People are usually better at recognizing and telling apart faces from their own racial group than faces from another group. The effect is not just a verbal belief that “they all look alike” — it shows up in actual memory and discrimination performance.

biases.name: Group Attribution Error
biases.description: People overgeneralize between individuals and groups: one member's traits get projected onto the whole group, and a group's actions get projected back onto each member. The shortcut feels efficient but can flatten real within-group differences.

biases.name: In-Group Bias
biases.description: Simply sorting people into 'us' and 'them' can skew trust, generosity, cooperation, and whose perspective gets believed. Designers run into it whenever identity cues change how fairly people are treated.

biases.name: Out-Group Homogeneity Bias
biases.description: People tend to see members of an out-group as more alike than members of their own group. 'They are all the same' becomes the default impression more easily than it does for 'us'.

biases.name: Prejudice
biases.description: Prejudice is a pre-judged evaluation of a social group or its members, where category membership drives liking, dislike, suspicion, or threat perception before individual evidence does. In practice it is broader than one single bias effect: it bundles attitudes, feelings, and judgment tendencies toward groups.

biases.name: Ultimate Attribution Error
biases.description: In intergroup settings, people often give their own group more charitable causal stories than the out-group: bad acts by “them” look dispositional, while good acts by “them” get explained away as luck or exception. It is a specifically intergroup version of attribution bias, with prejudice embedded in the explanation pattern.

topics.name: Liking
topics.description: Cialdini's Liking principle: people are more easily persuaded by requesters they like, driven by similarity, praise/ingratiation, cooperation, and mere familiarity/exposure.

biases.name: Liking Principle
biases.description: People are more easily persuaded by, and more likely to comply with requests from, people they like -- including people they like for reasons unrelated to the request itself, such as fleeting attraction, flattery, similarity, or shared cooperative effort.

topics.name: Marketplace Reputation Systems & Trust
topics.description: How online reputation/rating systems form and are interpreted in anonymous buyer-seller marketplace transactions, and how transaction-environment uncertainty shapes trust and rating behavior.

standalone_findings.description: In a modified investment-game experiment modeling anonymous online-market transactions, the existence of a reputation mechanism was associated with the overall decision of whether to transact in the marketplace, while specific reputation information shaped purchase decisions about particular sellers. Aggregate reputation information was weighted differently from singular reputation information, and as reputation signals became noisier buyers were less likely to react negatively to poor ratings and more likely to give sellers the benefit of the doubt after seemingly uncooperative outcomes.
standalone_findings.source_title: Reputation and Uncertainty in Online Markets: An Experimental Study

topics.name: Mere Exposure Effect
topics.description: Whether repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking for it with no reward or conscious evaluation required — the psychology behind familiar-pattern and repeated-branding arguments in design, and its real boundary condition (satiation/boredom at very high exposure counts).

biases.name: Mere Exposure Effect
biases.description: Repeated exposure to a stimulus can increase liking or preference even without reward or deeper evaluation. Familiarity itself can make a design, message, or brand element feel better.

standalone_findings.description: The exposure-liking relationship is not linear without limit: it follows an inverted-U shape, and very high numbers of exposures can trigger satiation/boredom that reduces or reverses the effect — a real boundary condition against a naive 'more repetition is always better' reading, directly relevant to how often a design pattern/brand element should actually be repeated.
standalone_findings.source_title: Exposure and Affect: Overview and Meta-Analysis of Research, 1968-1987

topics.name: Narrative Transportation & Storytelling Persuasion
topics.description: Green & Brock's theory that the more absorbed ('transported') a reader becomes in a narrative, the more their beliefs shift toward the story's implications — relevant to UX writing and marketing copy that uses storytelling as persuasion.

biases.name: Narrative Transportation
biases.description: Becoming absorbed into a story -- engaged imagery, affect, and attentional focus -- produces stronger shifts toward the story's own beliefs, more favorable views of its protagonists, and reduced scrutiny of factual inconsistencies within it.

topics.name: Persuasive Systems Design (PSD Framework)
topics.description: A structured framework (the PSD model) for designing and evaluating software specifically intended to change user behavior, distinct from general HCI usability frameworks.

standalone_findings.description: Proposes the Persuasive Systems Design (PSD) framework — a structured model for designing and evaluating software intended to change user attitudes or behavior, covering underlying design postulates, analysis of the persuasion context, and categorized system-feature types (primary task support, dialogue support, system credibility support, social support).
standalone_findings.source_title: Persuasive Systems Design: Key Issues, Process Model, and System Features
standalone_findings.source_venue: Communications of the Association for Information Systems

topics.name: Persuasive Technology / Captology
topics.description: The foundational academic field ('captology') studying how computers and interactive technology can be designed to change attitudes or behavior.

standalone_findings.description: Establishes 'captology' — the study of computers as persuasive technologies — proposing that persuasive computers function as tools, media, or social actors (the 'Functional Triad'), operate across individual-to-societal levels of analysis, and raise inherent ethical issues in designing technology intended to change attitudes or behavior.
standalone_findings.source_title: Persuasive computers: perspectives and research directions
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI)

topics.name: Power Posing
topics.description: The (contested) claim that adopting expansive body postures causes measurable hormonal and behavioral changes.

biases.name: Power Posing
biases.description: The popular claim that briefly holding an expansive, 'high-power' body posture changes a person's hormone levels (raising testosterone, lowering cortisol) and increases their real-world risk tolerance and confidence -- one of psychology's most publicly famous claims (via a widely-viewed TED talk), and one of its most publicly disputed.

standalone_findings.description: Adopting expansive ('high-power') body postures for brief periods caused measurable increases in testosterone, decreases in cortisol, and increased self-reported feelings of power and risk tolerance, compared to contractive ('low-power') postures.
standalone_findings.source_title: Power Posing: Brief Nonverbal Displays Affect Neuroendocrine Levels and Risk Tolerance

topics.name: Psychological Reactance
topics.description: People resist or reverse a persuasion attempt when they perceive their freedom of choice as being threatened — directly relevant to why heavy-handed persuasive/dark-pattern tactics can backfire.

biases.name: Reactance
biases.description: When people feel their freedom or autonomy is being threatened, they resist, push back, or sometimes do the opposite of what is being urged. Pressure can reduce compliance precisely because it feels controlling.

biases.name: Reverse Psychology
biases.description: A persuader deliberately recommends or allows the opposite of the desired outcome in hopes that the target will push back and choose the originally desired behavior instead. It is a tactic, not a basic cognitive mechanism by itself.

topics.name: Reciprocity
topics.description: Whether an unsolicited small gift or favor makes someone more likely to comply with a later request — directly relevant to 'free trial'/'free gift' design patterns, demonstrated concretely in a restaurant tipping field experiment.

biases.name: Reciprocity
biases.description: People feel obligated to return favors, gifts, or concessions — including small, unsolicited ones — which increases compliance with a subsequent request.

standalone_findings.description: A meta-analysis of 78 independent studies of the door-in-the-face compliance technique (a reciprocal-concessions application of the reciprocity principle: a large initial request is refused, then a smaller 'concession' request follows) found a significant effect on verbal compliance (agreeing to the request, r=.126) -- but, from 39 studies measuring actual behavioral compliance (following through on the agreement), the effect was not statistically significant (r=.052). The technique worked better for prosocial causes, for volunteering/research requests than monetary donations, and less well as the baseline difficulty of the request increased.
standalone_findings.source_title: The Door-in-the-Face Persuasive Message Strategy: A Meta-Analysis of the First 35 Years

topics.name: Scarcity & Urgency Messaging
topics.description: How limited-availability framing (real or implied) increases perceived value and purchase intent — and its direct line to manipulative urgency messaging.

biases.name: Scarcity Principle
biases.description: Limited availability (real or implied) of an option increases its perceived value and desirability.

topics.name: Social Comparison
topics.description: The drive to evaluate one's own opinions and abilities by comparing to others when no objective standard exists — the theoretical basis for leaderboards and social-proof indicators, with a genuinely current (2026) meta-analysis quantifying its real psychological cost in social-media contexts specifically.

biases.name: Bias Blind Spot
biases.description: People readily spot bias in other people while seeing their own judgments as comparatively objective. The mind gives itself a special exemption from the very distortions it recognizes elsewhere.

biases.name: Contrast Effect
biases.description: Judgments of an option, person, or price shift depending on what was seen just before or beside it, so the same target can feel better or worse by comparison. Relative context changes evaluation even when the focal item itself is unchanged.

biases.name: False Consensus Effect
biases.description: People overestimate how many other people share their own beliefs, choices, or habits. Our own view feels more normal and representative than it really is.

biases.name: Illusory Superiority
biases.description: People often rate their own abilities, traits, or judgment as better than average, even when that cannot be true for most of a group at once. Self-evaluation drifts upward when comparison targets are vague or flattering.

biases.name: Naïve Cynicism
biases.description: People can overestimate how biased, strategic, or self-interested other people's judgments are. Suspicion itself becomes biased, so disagreement gets read as ulterior motive faster than reality warrants.

biases.name: Social Comparison
biases.description: People evaluate their own standing, abilities, and outcomes by comparing themselves to others, and this comparison shapes emotional response and subsequent behavior — particularly upward comparison, which can produce either motivation or maladjustment depending on context.

biases.name: Spotlight Effect
biases.description: People overestimate how much other people notice their appearance, mistakes, and behavior. Our own experience is so vivid to us that we assume it is much more visible to everyone else than it really is.

topics.name: Social Norms (Descriptive/Injunctive)
topics.description: How descriptive norms (what others actually do) and injunctive norms (what others approve of) independently shape behavior, and what happens when they conflict.

biases.name: Social Proof
biases.description: People look to others' behavior (what most people actually do) to decide their own actions, especially under uncertainty.

standalone_findings.description: A meta-analysis found descriptive norms predict behavioral intentions with a medium-to-strong correlation and explain additional variance in intention beyond the standard theory-of-planned-behaviour predictors (attitude, subjective/injunctive norm, perceived behavioural control) -- independent, meta-analytic-scale confirmation that descriptive norms (the mechanism underlying social proof) genuinely predict behavior, not just a single-study demonstration. The relationship was found to be stronger for younger samples and for health-risk behaviors specifically.
standalone_findings.source_title: Descriptive norms as an additional predictor in the theory of planned behaviour: A meta-analysis

standalone_findings.description: Two field experiments found that descriptive-norm appeals ('the majority of guests reuse their towels') produced higher hotel-towel-reuse rates than a traditional appeal focused solely on environmental protection -- an independent replication of the descriptive-norms social-proof mechanism in a completely different real-world domain than the original littering-norms study. A further refinement, 'provincial norms' (describing behavior specific to the guest's own immediate setting, e.g. 'in this room'), was found to be even more effective than a generic descriptive-norm appeal.
standalone_findings.source_title: A Room with a Viewpoint: Using Social Norms to Motivate Environmental Conservation in Hotels

topics.name: Social Priming & the Replication Crisis
topics.description: Claims that subtle environmental or linguistic cues unconsciously shift subsequent behavior — one of the areas hit hardest by the replication crisis.

standalone_findings.description: Daniel Kahneman publicly acknowledged serious doubts about the replicability of social priming research — including specific studies (e.g. the 'Florida effect' walking-speed study) that he had cited approvingly in Thinking, Fast and Slow — and urged the field to address the problem directly.
standalone_findings.source_title: Nobel laureate challenges psychologists to clean up their act

topics.name: Trust Signals & Perceived Security Cues in UI
topics.description: What visual elements — security badges, HTTPS indicators, third-party seals — actually influence users' trust and willingness to transact online. Not all seals are equal: only a seal consumers actually recognize moves purchase probability.

biases.name: Trust Signals
biases.description: Visible cues intended to signal safety or legitimacy (third-party trust seals, security badges, credential stacking) can lower perceived risk and increase purchase intent -- but the effect is conditional rather than automatic: it depends on the viewer's own psychological state and on whether the specific seal is one the viewer actually recognizes.

topics.name: Unity
topics.description: Cialdini's Unity principle (the 6th/7th principle added in the 2016 revised edition of Influence): shared group identity, not mere interpersonal liking, as a distinct persuasion lever — 'we' framing changes influence through self-categorization rather than personal affinity.

biases.name: Unity Principle
biases.description: People are more readily influenced by others they perceive as sharing their identity or group membership ('we-ness') -- a distinct mechanism from ordinary liking, explained by shared identity making a source's norms and requests feel self-relevant rather than merely likeable.

domains.name: Value, Loss & Money Framing
domains.description: How the same option is valued differently depending on how it's described or coded, independent of the option set itself.

topics.name: Anchoring Effects
topics.description: How exposure to an initial number or value skews subsequent judgments and valuations, even when that anchor is arbitrary.

biases.name: Anchoring Bias
biases.description: Initial exposure to a number or value ('anchor') skews subsequent judgments and valuations toward that anchor, even when the anchor is arbitrary or irrelevant.

topics.name: Contrast Effect
topics.description: Judgment of a stimulus shifts based on comparison with a recently-encountered different stimulus, independent of the stimulus's own absolute properties — highly relevant to pricing and comparison-table UI design.

biases.name: Contrast Effect
biases.description: Judgments of an option, person, or price shift depending on what was seen just before or beside it, so the same target can feel better or worse by comparison. Relative context changes evaluation even when the focal item itself is unchanged.

topics.name: Cross-Cultural Variation in Loss Aversion
topics.description: Whether loss aversion's magnitude is a universal human parameter or varies systematically with culture — a 53-country survey found it varies predictably with individualism, power distance, masculinity, and religious composition.

biases.name: Loss Aversion
biases.description: Losses loom psychologically larger than equivalent gains — people work harder to avoid losing something than to gain the equivalent.

topics.name: Decoy Effect / Attraction Effect
topics.description: How adding an inferior third option can shift preference toward one of the original two options — and how consistently this actually replicates across contexts.

biases.name: Decoy Effect
biases.description: Adding a third option that is clearly inferior to one existing option (but not the other) increases the choice share of the option it's inferior to, violating rational-choice regularity.

topics.name: Disposition Effect
topics.description: Investors' tendency to sell appreciating assets too early while holding depreciating assets too long, relative to a rational expected-value strategy.

biases.name: Disposition Effect
biases.description: People can become more willing to lock in gains than to realize losses, selling winners too early while holding losers too long. The current gain/loss status of an option distorts exit decisions.

standalone_findings.description: In a field study of real investor trading data tracked from the start of individuals' investing careers, Feng & Seasholes independently confirm the core disposition-effect asymmetry (reluctance to realize losses, propensity to realize gains) that Weber & Camerer demonstrated in a lab task. A genuine refinement not present in the original: investor sophistication and trading experience together eliminate the loss-realization reluctance entirely, but only reduce the gain-realization propensity by 37% without eliminating it -- the two components of the disposition effect respond differently to experience.
standalone_findings.source_title: Do Investor Sophistication and Trading Experience Eliminate Behavioral Biases in Financial Markets?

topics.name: Endowment Effect
topics.description: The finding (and its methodological critique) that people value something more once they own it, demanding more to give it up than they'd pay to acquire it.

biases.name: Endowment Effect
biases.description: People demand more to give up something they own than they would pay to acquire the same thing — ownership itself inflates perceived value.

topics.name: IKEA Effect / Labor-Leads-to-Love Valuation
topics.description: The finding that self-assembled or self-created products are valued more highly than equivalent pre-made ones — conditional on successful completion.

biases.name: IKEA Effect
biases.description: People who build/assemble a product themselves value it more highly than an equivalent pre-made product — but only if the build is completed successfully.

standalone_findings.description: A 3-study developmental series found the IKEA effect emerges at age 5, coinciding with self-concept formation milestones -- but neither the amount of effort invested (Study 2) nor feelings of ownership (Study 3) explained why children valued their own creations more, explicitly finding these results incompatible with existing theories of the IKEA bias (effort-justification and psychological-ownership accounts). Proposes instead that the effect reflects a link between one's creations and one's self-concept.
standalone_findings.source_title: When and how does labour lead to love? The ontogeny and mechanisms of the IKEA effect

standalone_findings.description: A direct conceptual replication of the original IKEA-effect willingness-to-pay paradigm confirmed the effect's robustness and identified psychological ownership as the underlying psychological mechanism.
standalone_findings.source_title: The IKEA Effect. A Conceptual Replication

standalone_findings.description: In a longitudinal study of 924 parent-child dyads, involving children in cooking activities increased their liking of vegetables and, mediated through that liking, their vegetable intake -- a real-world, public-health-relevant field application of the IKEA effect. The effect held for children specifically; involvement did not similarly predict parents' own vegetable liking or intake.
standalone_findings.source_title: Cooking together: The IKEA effect on family vegetable intake

topics.name: Loss Aversion & Framing
topics.description: The finding that losses are weighted more heavily than equivalent gains in decision-making, and the framing effects this produces.

biases.name: Disposition Effect
biases.description: People can become more willing to lock in gains than to realize losses, selling winners too early while holding losers too long. The current gain/loss status of an option distorts exit decisions.

biases.name: Endowment Effect
biases.description: People demand more to give up something they own than they would pay to acquire the same thing — ownership itself inflates perceived value.

biases.name: Framing Effect
biases.description: Equivalent options can lead to different choices depending on how they are described—for example as gains versus losses—even when the underlying outcomes are unchanged. Presentation changes judgment, not just cosmetics.

biases.name: Loss Aversion
biases.description: Losses loom psychologically larger than equivalent gains — people work harder to avoid losing something than to gain the equivalent.

biases.name: Pseudocertainty Effect
biases.description: When an earlier uncertainty is framed as already resolved, people can treat a later probabilistic outcome as if it were effectively certain, even though the total net probability has not changed. The path to the outcome changes its psychological weight.

standalone_findings.description: Across four studies (assembling IKEA furniture, origami, Lego sets), people who built a product themselves valued it as highly as experts' finished creations and expected others to share that inflated valuation — but this effect only occurs when labor results in successful completion; it disappears if the built object is destroyed or left unfinished, and occurs equally for novices and experienced 'do-it-yourselfers.'
standalone_findings.source_title: The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love

topics.name: Mental Accounting
topics.description: Thaler's finding that people categorize and treat money differently depending on its source or intended use, rather than treating it as fully fungible — the psychological basis for budgeting categories, 'found money' spending, and windfall framing effects.

biases.name: Denomination Effect
biases.description: People are less willing to spend an equivalent amount of money when it is held in one large denomination than when it is split into smaller units. Large bills feel less 'spendable' and can function like a soft self-control device.

biases.name: Disposition Effect
biases.description: People can become more willing to lock in gains than to realize losses, selling winners too early while holding losers too long. The current gain/loss status of an option distorts exit decisions.

biases.name: Mental Accounting
biases.description: People categorize and treat money differently depending on its source or intended use, rather than treating it as fully fungible.

standalone_findings.description: Testing a 'double-entry' mental accounting model (which assumes payments generate an immediate psychological 'pain of paying' that is buffered when payment is decoupled from consumption in time or salience) against a standard discounted-utility model on a set of consumer financing scenarios, the double-entry model provided a better fit of subjects' stated preferences for 60% of subjects, versus 29% for the discounting model (even allowing the discounting model positive or negative discount rates).
standalone_findings.effect_size: 60% of subjects better fit by double-entry mental accounting model vs. 29% by discounted-utility model
standalone_findings.source_title: The Red and the Black: Mental Accounting of Savings and Debt

topics.name: Money Illusion
topics.description: People reason about money in nominal terms rather than inflation-adjusted real terms, letting purely nominal framing change financial judgments and decisions.

biases.name: Money Illusion
biases.description: People often judge money by its face value rather than its real purchasing power. Nominal numbers can feel like gains or losses even when the underlying economic value says otherwise.

topics.name: Pain of Paying
topics.description: The psychological discomfort of paying varies by payment method and format — cash triggers more 'pain' than card or digital payment — which is why less-salient payment methods tend to increase spending.

biases.name: Pain of Paying
biases.description: Making a payment generates an immediate psychological cost that is separate from the economic cost of the purchase -- and this 'pain' is buffered or sharpened depending on how tightly payment is coupled, in time and salience, to the consumption it finances.

topics.name: Placebo Effects
topics.description: A person experiences a genuine change in symptoms or performance from an inert treatment or manipulation, driven by expectation rather than any active ingredient or mechanism.

biases.name: Placebo Effect
biases.description: Expectations and treatment context can change what people actually feel or report, even when the intervention itself is inert. But the broad popular idea of a placebo 'working' across all outcomes is stronger than the best evidence supports.

topics.name: Price/Marketing Placebo Effects & Expectation-Driven Experience
topics.description: Whether price and marketing cues change genuine subjective — and sometimes measurable neural — experience of a product or service, independent of any real difference in the product itself. Directly relevant to premium pricing and polished visual design shaping perceived quality before any actual use.

biases.name: Expectation Bias
biases.description: What people expect beforehand can alter what they later feel, notice, or report about the same experience. Prior cues such as price, branding, warnings, or promises can bias downstream judgments so the product seems better or worse before anything objective has changed.

biases.name: Price Placebo Effect
biases.description: Price and other marketing cues can change the experience itself, not just what people say about it afterward. A 'premium' frame can make the same product feel more effective, pleasant, or valuable.

topics.name: Pseudocertainty Effect
topics.description: Treating a probabilistic outcome as though it were certain when it's framed as resolving a prior source of uncertainty, even though the actual net probability is unchanged.

biases.name: Pseudocertainty Effect
biases.description: When an earlier uncertainty is framed as already resolved, people can treat a later probabilistic outcome as if it were effectively certain, even though the total net probability has not changed. The path to the outcome changes its psychological weight.

topics.name: Scarcity & Urgency Messaging
topics.description: How limited-availability framing (real or implied) increases perceived value and purchase intent — and its direct line to manipulative urgency messaging.

biases.name: Scarcity Principle
biases.description: Limited availability (real or implied) of an option increases its perceived value and desirability.

topics.name: Zero-Price Effect
topics.description: Demand for a free item is disproportionately higher than its price-discount alone would predict — 'FREE!' exerts an extra pull on choice beyond what standard demand curves account for.

biases.name: Zero-Price Effect
biases.description: Demand for a free item is disproportionately higher than its price-discount alone would predict — 'FREE!' exerts an extra pull on choice beyond what standard demand curves account for.

standalone_findings.description: Across 3 experiments, time pressure was found to REDUCE (not intensify) preference for a free product version in freemium digital-product contexts, when time-pressure-induced anchoring effects were directed appropriately -- mediated by the perceived performance risk of the product, with an upper boundary condition for monetary price level identified. A genuine, empirically demonstrated exception to the usual zero-price pull, not a universal effect.
standalone_findings.source_title: When time pressure counters the zero price effect

standalone_findings.description: In a two-component tourism product (hotel room plus breakfast), even though consumers preferred their more expensive alternative, offering a free breakfast on the cheaper option shifted demand toward it and away from the pricier option -- despite the total price gap. Demonstrates the zero-price effect is not confined to single-product comparisons but generalizes to multicomponent bundling contexts, directly relevant to 'free add-on' and bundling design in pricing UX.
standalone_findings.source_title: The Free Breakfast Effect

domains.name: Visual & Aesthetic Perception
domains.description: How visual/sensory design is processed and judged.

topics.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
topics.description: The finding that users perceive more visually appealing interfaces as more usable even when actual usability is held constant — the 'what is beautiful is usable' effect, and how reliably it replicates across different samples and study designs.

biases.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
biases.description: Visually appealing designs are often perceived as easier to use, and can genuinely improve task performance under certain conditions.

topics.name: Aesthetics & Task Performance
topics.description: Whether and when visually appealing design actually improves task performance, versus simply being preferred.

biases.name: Aesthetic-Usability Effect
biases.description: Visually appealing designs are often perceived as easier to use, and can genuinely improve task performance under certain conditions.

topics.name: Cognitive Bias Taxonomies for Design Practice
topics.description: Academic attempts to organize the large, diffuse space of cognitive biases into taxonomies usable by a specific design discipline (e.g. data visualization), rather than by abstract cognitive theory — the direct precedent for this project's own BiasHeuristic taxonomy.

standalone_findings.description: Proposes a task-based taxonomy of 154 cognitive biases relevant to information visualization design, organized into 7 categories by which analysis/visualization task they affect — explicitly built to be more usable for designers than prior bias taxonomies organized around abstract cognitive theory, while noting limited empirical research documents how most of these biases actually affect real visual data analysis activities.
standalone_findings.source_title: A Task-Based Taxonomy of Cognitive Biases for Information Visualization
standalone_findings.source_venue: IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics

topics.name: Color Psychology in Design
topics.description: Whether specific colors reliably produce specific emotional or behavioral responses in design contexts — real color-emotion associations exist, but the strongest available reviews explicitly decline to support conversion-rate claims, making this a close cousin of the F-Pattern/Jakob's-Law pattern of popular folklore outrunning the evidence.

standalone_findings.description: Across 132 studies spanning 1895–2022 and 42,266 participants in 64 countries, colors show systematic, reliable associations with affective dimensions (valence, arousal, power) and discrete emotion terms — e.g. red with high-arousal empowering emotions, blue/green with positive low-arousal emotions. However, the authors explicitly note these correspondences were tested mostly at an abstract, associative level, and 'it remains to be seen whether such correspondences translate to the impact of colour on experienced emotions and specific contexts' — i.e. this review does not validate that these associations reliably drive real-world behavior (such as marketing conversion) in applied UI/design contexts.
standalone_findings.source_title: Do we feel colours? A systematic review of 128 years of psychological research linking colours and emotions

standalone_findings.description: Across four studies, individual hues map onto distinct brand-personality dimensions (e.g. red toward excitement, blue toward competence/trust, consistent with Aaker's brand personality framework), and saturation/value amplify these effects; in a controlled experiment, strategically chosen color shifted brand personality perception and purchase intent. This is the closest thing in this batch to the popular 'red = urgency, blue = trust' marketing claim, but it comes from a single paper (no independent replication found), and its own framing is about brand-personality perception shifting in controlled conditions — not a general, context-free 'this color increases conversion' rule.
standalone_findings.source_title: Exciting red and competent blue: the importance of color in marketing
standalone_findings.source_venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

standalone_findings.description: Color can carry meaning and influence affect, cognition, and behavior, but the empirical literature on color psychology 'remains at a nascent stage of development' — the authors explicitly state that considerable further work on boundary conditions, moderators, and real-world generalizability is needed 'before strong conceptual statements and recommendations for application are warranted.' This directly cautions against confident practitioner claims (e.g. that a specific color reliably produces a specific behavioral/conversion outcome) that go beyond what the evidence at the time supported.
standalone_findings.source_title: Color Psychology: Effects of Perceiving Color on Psychological Functioning in Humans

topics.name: Eye-Tracking & Visual Scanning Patterns
topics.description: How people's eyes actually move across a page or screen while reading or searching — F-shaped, Z-shaped, or otherwise — and how that pattern depends on the content type (text-heavy vs. image-heavy) and task (browsing vs. searching), rather than being a single universal law.

biases.name: F-Pattern (Reading)
biases.description: Users scan web content in a rough F-shaped pattern: two horizontal sweeps across the top of the content area, then a vertical scan down the left side, reading progressively less as they go.

standalone_findings.description: Eye-movement analysis of web-text skim-reading under time pressure found readers explicitly direct attention to the most important information and improve memory-test performance as a result, achieved by 'satisficing' -- reading a section until the rate of information gain drops below a threshold, then skipping ahead to the next section. Gaze patterns at both paragraph and page level supported this explanation, offering an independent mechanistic account for declining-attention reading patterns on web pages.
standalone_findings.source_title: Skim reading by satisficing
standalone_findings.source_venue: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '11)

topics.name: Gestalt Principles in Interface Design
topics.description: The classic perceptual-grouping principles (proximity, similarity, closure, common region, figure-ground) as applied to visual and interaction design, distinct from the original 1920s Gestalt psychology literature they're derived from.

biases.name: Gestalt Principles
biases.description: People read interfaces as grouped, continuous, and complete patterns rather than as isolated parts. Gestalt principles help designers make structure legible at a glance.

biases.name: Law of Common Region
biases.description: Elements enclosed within the same bounded area are perceived as belonging together. Containers, cards, shaded panels, and section backgrounds all exploit this grouping cue in interface design.

biases.name: Law of Proximity
biases.description: Elements placed near one another are more likely to be perceived as belonging together. Spacing itself communicates structure before labels or borders do.

biases.name: Law of Prägnanz
biases.description: When several organizations are possible, perception tends to settle on the simplest, most stable overall form the stimulus supports. Designers invoke it when reducing clutter helps people 'see the pattern' faster.

biases.name: Law of Similarity
biases.description: Elements that look alike in color, shape, size, type style, or another visual property are perceived as belonging together. Visual sameness acts like an implicit label.

biases.name: Law of Uniform Connectedness
biases.description: Elements that are visibly connected by the same region, line, container, or filled background tend to be seen as a single unit before looser grouping cues are considered. Explicit connection usually outranks mere spacing or similarity.

topics.name: Progressive Disclosure
topics.description: The design pattern of surfacing only necessary or requested information at each step and deferring advanced options — including evidence that its benefits are context-dependent rather than universally positive.

biases.name: Progressive Disclosure
biases.description: Presenting only the information or controls needed for the immediate task, deferring less-common options and complexity to secondary views revealed on request, on the working assumption that simplifying what's shown up front improves usability without removing capability.

topics.name: Typography & Legibility (Typeface, Line Length, Reading Comprehension)
topics.description: Whether typeface choice, font size, or line length actually affects reading speed and comprehension the way common design folklore claims — including a genuinely current (2026) study directly complicating the 'serif for print, sans-serif for screen' convention.

standalone_findings.description: Comparing Verdana (sans-serif) against Times New Roman (serif), each read either on screen or on paper, Millhagen et al. found no interaction between font type and reading format on text comprehension: sans-serif conferred no specific advantage on screen, nor serif on paper. Comprehension was overall higher and cognitive load lower when reading on screen regardless of font type. The result directly complicates the common design-practice claim that serif fonts should be used for print and sans-serif fonts for screens.
standalone_findings.source_title: Just the font types? Effects of serif vs. sans-serif font types on text comprehension in screen vs. paper reading

standalone_findings.description: Comparing a medium (~55 characters per line) versus a long (~100 characters per line) line length for on-screen reading, Dyson and Haselgrove found the medium line length produced better comprehension scores than the long line length, at both normal and fast reading speeds. Reading fast reduced overall comprehension relative to normal speed, but did not change the type of information recalled (main ideas vs. incidental facts vs. structure), and the comprehension difference was not offset by a speed/accuracy trade-off.
standalone_findings.source_title: The influence of reading speed and line length on the effectiveness of reading from screen

standalone_findings.description: Using a purpose-built parametric typeface that varied only in serif size (0%, 5%, 10% of cap height, all else held constant), Arditi and Cho found no significant difference in reading speed between serif and sans-serif variants under RSVP or continuous paper reading. A small legibility (acuity-threshold) advantage did appear for the 5%-serif variant, but it was smaller than what the increased inter-letter spacing serifs themselves impose would predict — meaning the effect is attributable to spacing, not to the serif shape per se — and the authors report no legibility difference attributable to serifs as such.
standalone_findings.source_title: Serifs and font legibility

topics.name: Uncanny Valley
topics.description: Whether emotional response to human-like artificial characters plunges sharply just short of true realism before recovering — proposed in an obscure 1970 essay, now confirmed at scale by the first meta-analysis of the effect (large effect size), directly relevant to AI-avatar and chatbot design.

biases.name: Uncanny Valley
biases.description: As an artificial character's human likeness increases, emotional response grows more positive -- until, just short of true human likeness, it plunges sharply into revulsion and unease, before recovering again once likeness becomes genuinely indistinguishable from a real human.

topics.name: Visual Clutter & Interface Complexity
topics.description: How measurable visual clutter/complexity in an interface affects processing — the empirical grounding for minimalist-design guidance, distinct from the separate Aesthetic-Usability Effect.

biases.name: Aesthetic and Minimalist Design
biases.description: Interfaces should minimize irrelevant or competing information so important content and actions remain salient. In Nielsen's sense, this is mainly a clutter-reduction principle, not the separate claim that beauty itself automatically makes things more usable.

topics.name: Weber's Law / Just Noticeable Difference
topics.description: Whether a stimulus change only becomes perceptible once it crosses a fixed proportion of the current magnitude — the basis for 'gradual, below-threshold changes go unnoticed' design/pricing folklore, genuinely disputed by neural-coding evidence favoring a linear rather than logarithmic relationship.

biases.name: Weber's Law / Just Noticeable Difference
biases.description: A change becomes noticeable only once it exceeds a threshold relative to the current stimulus level — the classic just-noticeable-difference idea. Designers often use it to reason about how much visual, motion, haptic, or pricing change users will actually perceive.

standalone_findings.description: Reviews how psychophysical models of perceptual imprecision (the Weber's-law lineage: judgments become less precise as stimulus magnitude increases) can be adapted to model imprecision in economic decision-making, since real choice behavior is much less precise than traditional decision theory assumes. Applies this framework to stochastic choice, choice under risk, decoy effects in marketing, and delayed price adjustment -- directly connecting the classic psychophysical construct to design-relevant pricing and choice-architecture contexts.
standalone_findings.source_title: Modeling Imprecision in Perception, Valuation, and Choice

topics.name: Uncategorized
topics.description: Not yet assigned a topic.

biases.name: Appeal to Probability Fallacy
biases.description: People treat a possible or vaguely probable scenario as if it were effectively certain or already true. The move is common in speculation, risk talk, and product storytelling: 'it could happen' quietly becomes 'it will happen.'

biases.name: Argument from Fallacy
biases.description: A claim gets dismissed just because one argument for it was flawed, as if a bad argument automatically proves the conclusion false. That is a reasoning mistake about arguments, not strong evidence of a distinct named cognitive-bias effect.

biases.name: Delmore Effect
biases.description: A claimed tendency to formulate clearer, more articulate goals for narrow or lower-priority areas than for broader, higher-stakes ambitions. The label's exact meaning varies across internet bias lists.

biases.name: Masked Man Fallacy
biases.description: A reasoner substitutes one label for another inside a belief- or knowledge-based context as if identity automatically preserves truth, even when the person in the story would not make that substitution. It is a textbook logic problem about reference and knowledge, not a clearly established named cognitive-bias effect.

biases.name: Murphy's Law
biases.description: 'Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong' is a memorable engineering aphorism about planning for failure and edge cases, not a tested behavioral-science finding. In design practice it functions as a resilience mindset more than a psychological law.

biases.name: Postel's Law
biases.description: Be liberal in what you accept from others, conservative in what you send — applied in UX to mean interfaces should tolerate messy user input while producing clean, predictable output.

biases.name: Pro-Innovation Bias
biases.description: People or organizations can overvalue novelty, assuming a new technology, feature, or process is good mainly because it is innovative. The bias shows up when limits, harms, maintenance cost, or user fit are underweighted in the excitement of the new.
